article.authors: Wenrun Zhu; Yajie Niu; Guirong Liu; Xiang Yu; Hui Yin; Shuanghui Tang; Yunjun Liu; Jiu Wang
article.abstract: Abstract The anticancer efficacy of iridium(III) complexes has been extensively studied. A new ligand TFMPIP (2-(4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl)-1H-imidazo[4,5-f][1,10]phenanthroline) and its four iridium(III) complexes [Ir(C−N)2(TFMPIP)]PF6 (C−N = ppy: 13a, bzq: 13b, piq: 13c, and dfppy: 13d) were synthesized and characterized. The complexes show moderate or low cytotoxicity against LA795, HCT116, and Huh7 cells, while their liposome formulations 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo significantly enhanced the antiproliferative activity against LA795 cells. Mechanistic investigations revealed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo accumulated in mitochondria and induced pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction. Subsequent experiments confirmed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo triggered apoptosis, suppressed the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, and induced ferroptosis. In vivo antitumor activity showed that 13c@lipo significantly inhibited tumor growth in the LA795 tumor-bearing model with a high inhibitory rate of 82.72%. Collectively, these findings identify 13c@lipo as a promising liposomal Ir(III)-based candidate for lung adenocarcinoma therapy.

article.title: Lysosomal acidification through membrane contacts with mitochondria
article.authors: Zhiqi Tian; Yujie Sun; Jiajie Diao
article.abstract: Recent work from two independent studies has uncovered mitochondria as a previously unrecognized proton source driving lysosomal acidification. In this Viewpoint, we summarize these findings, examine the associated proteins and functional mechanisms, and discuss their relevance to disease.

article.title: Dietary high salt drives cognitive impairment and Aβ accumulation via an insufficient compensatory mitophagy response
article.authors: Jie Wen; Hao Ren; Fan Wen; Junping Yu; Haixia Fan; Jincheng Liu; Zhiyou Cai
article.abstract: There is mounting evidence that dietary habits are strongly correlated with cerebrovascular diseases and dementia, but the precise mechanism remains unclear how a salt-rich diet adversely affects the brain. Here, 12-month-old mice were fed a high-salt diet (HSD) for 2 months, and we observed salt-induced cognitive deficits in mice. The short-term HSD increased mitophagy-associated markers (PINK1, Parkin, and LC3-II) and decreased SQSTM1/p62, consistent with a compensatory mitophagy response that was insufficient to prevent cognitive decline. Neuro-2a cells were cultured in normal medium, NaCl medium (40 mM) or NaCl (40 mM) + CCCP group (20 μM) medium for 24 h, respectively. Short-term HSD feeding impaired learning and memory and increased amyloid-β (Aβ) burden, in parallel with altered PINK1/Parkin-associated mitophagy markers. These findings link a salt-rich diet to cognitive dysfunction, and suggest that enhancing PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy may counteract the harmful effects of HSD on the brain. Therefore, the PINK1/Parkin mitophagy may be a potential target for combating the harmful effects on the brain caused by HSD or other diseases related to mitophagy.

article.title: Synergistic regulation of neuroinflammation by mitophagy and the cGAS–STING pathway following ischemic stroke
article.authors: Yu Xiao; Peijie Fu; Chun Zhao; Wenqi Song; Yutao Lu; Huiqin Wang; Xiaoping Yin; Zhiying Chen; Yuanyuan Xiang
article.abstract: Neuroinflammation is widely recognized as a major driver of secondary brain injury following ischemic stroke. Recent studies have shown that mitochondrial dysfunction-induced mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release is one of the key mechanisms activating the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Mitophagy, as a quality control mechanism maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis, selectively clears damaged mitochondria, thereby limiting the leakage of abnormal mtDNA. Although previous reviews have outlined the general framework of the mitophagy-cGAS-STING interaction in neuroinflammation, this review places it within the specific context of ischemic stroke. It integrates the cell type-specificity of the neurovascular unit, explores both synergistic and interactive aspects, and evaluates targeted nanotherapeutic strategies. This article aims to explore the potential synergistic role of mitophagy and the cGAS-STING pathway in the pathological progression of ischemic stroke. First, the article elaborates on mitophagy and mitophagy-dependent regulation of neuroinflammation, highlighting its role in suppressing cGAS-STING activation by preventing mtDNA leakage. Second, it examines the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in neuroinflammation, with particular attention to cGAS-STING activation across neurovascular unit cell types (microglia, neurons, astrocytes, endothelial cells). Third, the functional synergy and potential molecular crosstalk between mitophagy and the cGAS–STING pathway in neuroinflammation are discussed. Finally, the article summarizes the potential therapeutic strategies targeting mitophagy and the cGAS-STING pathway, and further explores the emerging potential of microenvironment-responsive intelligent nanoplatforms to enhance drug delivery efficiency and multidimensional synergistic mechanisms by targeting the cGAS-STING pathway and mitochondria, thereby achieving precise immune regulation and improving therapeutic efficacy. This paper provides a mechanistic perspective on immune intervention for ischemic stroke and lays a theoretical foundation for future clinical translation strategies.

article.title: Xiaoai Jiedu recipe promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation by alleviating PINK1-mediated mitophagy in hepatocellular carcinoma
article.authors: Yuan-yuan Wu; Hui-ming Zhu; Zi-yu Lu; Zhuo-hui Tang; Wen-ting Li; Mian-hua Wu
article.abstract: Background The Xiaoai Jiedu recipe (XJR), a traditional Chinese medicinal formula, has been applied clinically for liver cancer management. XJR exhibits promising anti-tumor potential and may offer a novel strategy for oncological intervention. This study was designed to investigate the molecular mechanisms by which XJR exerts its pharmacological effects against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods In vivo assays were conducted employing an HCC xenograft mouse model, and HepG2 cells were employed in vitro . ELISA, immunohistochemistry (IHC), immunofluorescence (IF), RT-PCR and western blot were performed to detect PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1)-mediated mitophagy and NLRP3 (NOD-like receptor protein 3) inflammasome activation. The cellular mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were tested with DCFH-DA and MitoSOX. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and JC-1 were utilized to observe the mitochondrial morphology and function, as well as mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in the process of XJR intervention for HCC. Results XJR prominently promoted pyroptosis by upregulating the related inflammatory cytokines levels in serum and HepG2 cells. The key targets include PINK1, parkin, p62, LC3B, TOMM20, COX IV, NLRP3, ASC, GSDMD, caspase1, IL-1β and IL-18 were observed. XJR disrupted PINK1-mediated mitophagy, which in turn increased mitochondrial ROS levels and promoted NLRP3 inflammasome assembly both in vitro and in vivo . Meanwhile, functional assays using pathway-specific inhibitors and siRNA-mediated knockdown further demonstrated that XJR suppresses mitophagy and enhances NLRP3 inflammasome activation via inhibition of the PINK1/parkin signaling pathway. Conclusions The preliminary results of the present study suggested that XJR may alleviate PINK1-mediated mitophagy and motivate NLRP3 signaling pathway to subsequently exert anti-tumor effects in HCC.

article.title: SH3GLB1 mediates tumor cell resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors by regulating mitophagy
article.authors: Jianhua Lu; Hongzheng Li; Shengsheng Zhao; Kongqin Lu; Ji Lin; Xiaojiao Ruan; Bingzi Zhu; Letian Meng; Weiteng Zhang; Yongdong Yi; Danna Liang; Letian Chen; Ruan Yu; Gongting Zhou; Binglong Bai; Zhonglin Ni; Yuekai Cui; Luchen Sun; Hongbo Zhang; Xiangyang Xue; Xian Shen; Qiantong Dong; Zhaoyu Shen; Jessica M. Rosenholm; Shangrui Rao; Weijian Sun
article.abstract: Abstract Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been widely utilized in cancer treatment, but their effectiveness was often hampered by the development of drug resistance. A better understanding of the TKIs resistance mechanism is beneficial to improving therapeutic strategies. Our study found that SH3GLB1 expression was elevated in drug-resistant cells by transcriptome sequencing and correlated with poor prognosis. Silencing SH3GLB1 substantially abrogated TKIs resistance in tumor cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis demonstrated a strong correlation between SH3GLB1 and mitophagy. Subsequent experiments confirmed that elevated SH3GLB1 expression promoted TKIs-induced intracellular mitophagy, accompanied by decreased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, thereby attenuating TKIs-induced cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, we elucidated that SH3GLB1 interacted with the ATG5-ATG12-ATG16L1 complex to modulate mitophagic activity. Additionally, CDK1 expression was associated with changes in SH3GLB1 protein abundance and ubiquitination, suggesting a potential role for CDK1 in regulating SH3GLB1 stability. Collectively, our findings identify SH3GLB1 as a regulator of mitophagy-associated TKIs resistance in HCC cells. SH3GLB1 interacts with the ATG5-ATG12-ATG16L1 complex to promote mitochondrial clearance and reduce ROS accumulation, whereas CDK1 expression was associated with changes in SH3GLB1 ubiquitination and protein abundance, suggesting that CDK1 may participate in the regulation of SH3GLB1 protein stability. These findings suggest that targeting SH3GLB1 may represent a potential strategy for restoring TKIs sensitivity.

article.title: Scutellarein nanoparticles suppress colon cancer via PHB2-mediated mitophagy inhibition with modulatory effects on tumor-associated depression and osteotropic migration
article.authors: Yuanzhi Li; Hao Xu; Zonglin Cai; Shimei Liu; Xuqiang Luo; Jinghua Liang; Yingying Liao
article.abstract: Background Colorectal cancer progression involves mitophagy, in which Prohibitin 2 (PHB2) regulates the PARL–PGAM5–PINK1 axis. Scutellarein has antitumor activity but poor bioavailability. We developed integrin αvβ3-targeted β-cyclodextrin-based scutellarein nanoparticles (Scu-NPs), which enhance the solubility, stability, and tumor-targeting of scutellarein, and investigated whether they suppress colon cancer via PHB2-mediated mitophagy inhibition and modulate tumor-associated depression and osteotropic migration. Methods PHB2 expression and mitochondrial localization were examined in colon cancer cells. SW480 cells with PHB2 overexpression were treated with Scu or Scu-NPs. Proliferation, migration, invasion, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, and mitophagy-related proteins were assessed. Subcutaneous xenografts, a chronic unpredictable mild stress tumor–depression model, behavioral tests, osteotropic migration assays, and bioinformatics were used. Results PHB2 was highly expressed and mitochondria-localized in colon cancer cells. Scu-NPs downregulated PHB2, increased PARL, decreased PGAM5, PINK1, Parkin, and LC3-II/LC3-I, and increased P62, indicating mitophagy inhibition. Scu-NPs induced mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS accumulation, apoptosis, and inhibited proliferation, migration, and invasion; PHB2 overexpression partially reversed these effects. In vivo , Scu-NPs suppressed xenograft growth and improved depressive-like behaviors, with PHB2 overexpression attenuating these effects. In vitro , Scu-NPs reduced colon cancer cell migration toward osteoblast-conditioned medium, whereas PHB2 overexpression partially reversed this effect. Conclusion Scu-NPs suppress colon cancer by downregulating PHB2 and inhibiting mitophagy. PHB2 may serve as a shared molecular node linking tumor progression, depressive-like behaviors, and osteotropic migration, supporting Scu-NPs as a multi-target strategy.

article.title: A premature ovarian insufficiency-associated LMD-3 point mutation impairs protein stability and causes autophagic-lysosomal dysfunction in Caenorhabditis elegans
article.authors: Yile Zhai; Tiantian Wang; Meixi Gong; Yuhan Liang; Wenfei Li; Xin Wang; Zhe Zhang
article.abstract: Reproductive longevity decline characterizes both natural aging and premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). While our previous work established C. elegans LMD-3 as a critical regulator of reproductive capacity, the in vivo consequences of specific clinical mutations remain unclear. Here, we modeled the POI-associated human NCOA7 W804C mutation by engineering the orthologous W690C substitution into the C. elegans lmd-3 locus. We demonstrate that this single-nucleotide substitution severely compromises LMD-3 protein stability and reduces transcript levels. This mutational destabilization is associated with profound systemic autophagic-lysosomal dysfunction, which impairs macromolecular degradation and leads to widespread proteotoxic accumulation of misfolded proteins. Coincident with these organismal defects, mutant animals exhibit an early-onset collapse in reproductive capacity driven by elevated germline apoptosis. Crucially, this pathology is consistent with reduced vitamin B12 availability; mecobalamin supplementation can mitigate the lysosomal block, restoring autophagic flux, proteostasis, and fecundity. These findings elucidate how a clinical mutation drives systemic lysosomal failure and reproductive decline, suggesting vitamin B12 supplementation as a promising metabolic intervention worth further translational exploration.

article.title: Divergence of cortical force-generating mechanisms underlies differences in spindle behavior between C. elegans and C. inopinata
article.authors: Shun Oomura; Koji Kyoda; Shuichi Onami; Nami Haruta; Asako Sugimoto
article.abstract: Microtubule-dependent pronuclear migration and mitotic spindle positioning are fundamental processes during the first embryonic division in many animals. In the one-cell embryo of Caenorhabditis elegans , these events are regulated by well-characterized pulling forces acting on astral microtubules, including cortical forces mediated by the Gα-GPR-LIN-5 dynein complex. Although the overall framework of these dynamics is conserved, recent studies have revealed substantial interspecies variation in their regulation. Here, we investigated nuclei and mitotic spindle behaviors in one-cell embryos of Caenorhabditis inopinata , the closest known relative of C. elegans , using live-cell imaging and functional perturbation. We found that C. inopinata embryos exhibit altered pronuclear migration, reduced anaphase spindle oscillations, and slower centrosome diffusion during telophase compared with C. elegans . These differences suggest weaker cortical pulling forces. Functional analyses using RNA interference showed that GPR retains its essential role in force generation, whereas the contribution of the microtubule depolymerizing kinesin KLP-7 is reduced in C. inopinata . Our results point to evolutionary changes in microtubule-regulated spindle dynamics, and provide insight into how conserved cellular processes can diversify through subtle changes in their underlying mechanisms.

article.title: Laminophatic Mutations Affect SUN-1 Dynamics and Chromosome Pairing During C. elegans Meiosis
article.authors: Lenka Hůlková; Jana Petrusová; Petr Flachs; Tomáš Venit; Pavel Hozák
article.abstract: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes undergo dynamic movements to ensure correct pairing. This process depends on the LINC complex, which transmits cytoskeletal forces across the nuclear envelope via SUN domain proteins anchored in the inner nuclear membrane. Here, we demonstrate that lamin plays an essential role at the nuclear periphery during early prophase I. Using Caenorhabditis elegans as a model, we introduced mutations into the Ig domain of the lamin gene (CeLMN) that mimic human laminopathic variants. These mutations impaired SUN-1 dynamics at the nuclear envelope, leading to defects in homologous chromosome pairing and synaptonemal complex assembly. Specifically, laminopathic strains displayed abnormal SUN-1 mobility, incomplete loading of the central element protein SYP-1, and altered localization of the axial element protein HTP-3. As a consequence, meiotic nuclei frequently contained supernumerary 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-stained bodies and exhibited chromosomal aberrations during diakinesis. Our findings reveal a crucial role for the lamin Ig domain in coordinating nuclear mechanics with LINC complex function, thereby safeguarding chromosome dynamics and genome stability during gametogenesis.

article.title: Gut Microbiota Translocation Drives the Pathogenesis of Fatty Liver Syndrome via Disrupting Hepatic Metabolic Homeostasis in Laying Hens.
article.authors: Zhang-Chao Deng; En-Ling Wang; Yu Zhang; Zhi-Yuan Xia; Yu-Xuan Huang; Bing-Bing Zhang; Meng Liu; Ling Zhao; Lv-Hui Sun
article.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fatty liver syndrome (FLS) in laying hens is associated with gut dysbiosis. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to explore the underlying mechanism by which gut dysbiosis contributes to the pathogenesis of FLS in laying hens. METHODS: In Experiment 1, 68-wk-old laying hens, that were healthy or with FLS (n = 10 birds/group), were selected on the basis of pathological changes in liver morphology. In Experiment 2, 40-wk-old breeder hens (n = 16 birds/group) were given either a basal diet (CON) or CON supplemented with 1.5 kg/t organic acid blends (OA1 and OA2) for 12 weeks. The production performance, gut barrier integrity, hepatic histopathology, gene expression, and gut microbiota were analyzed. The omics data were analyzed using bioinformatics tools, while the other data were analyzed using Student's t-tests. RESULTS: Compared with healthy hens, FLS hens exhibited increases (P < 0.05) in total cholesterol (TC) and triglyceride (TG) levels in both the serum and liver by 69.9-267.8%, and their serum lipopolysaccharide levels increased (P < 0.05) by 27.3%. Integrated omics analysis revealed that the abundance of Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group increased (P < 0.05), whereas the pathways for histidine, glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism were inhibited in the livers of FLS hens. Furthermore, dietary supplementation with OA1 and/or OA2 reduced (P < 0.05) the incidence of deformed eggs by 21.1-25.8% during weeks 7 to 12, decreased (P < 0.05) liver TG and TC contents by 26.3-60.7% compared to the CON group. Meanwhile, OA1 and OA2 reduced (P < 0.05) serum lipopolysaccharide levels by 23.4-25.6%, while OA2 upregulated (P < 0.05) the expression of cecal tight junction gene Claudin-1 by 111.6%. CONCLUSIONS: FLS progression in aged laying hens is primarily due to increased gut barrier impairment and bacterial translocation. OA supplementation improved gut barrier integrity and mitigated the occurrence of FLS in hens.

article.title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells in ameliorating ovarian aging: Insights from single-cell analysis
article.authors: Jin-Ning Zhang; Shuang Tian; Xin-Meng Guo; Qi Zhang; Jin Shang; Yuan-Qing Yao
article.abstract: BACKGROUND Ovarian aging, characterized by follicle depletion and declining oocyte quality, significantly contributes to infertility in women of advanced maternal age. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) offer a promising therapeutic strategy, although their precise mechanisms of action remain poorly understood. AIM To investigate the therapeutic effects of umbilical cord-derived MSCs (UCMSCs) on ovarian aging and to elucidate the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms through single-cell transcriptomic analysis. METHODS Aged female ICR mice (10-11 months) were allocated into aged control and UCMSC transplantation (A-MSC) groups, along with young controls for comparison. A-MSC mice received tail vein injections of UCMSCs. Ovarian function was evaluated through estrous cycle monitoring, follicle counting, hormone assays, and assessment of oocyte quality (mitochondrial function, spindle morphology, aneuploidy). Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was conducted on ovarian tissues to analyze transcriptional changes, cell-cell communication, and granulosa cell (GC) trajectories. RESULTS Transplantation of UCMSCs resulted in improved estrous cycle regularity, increased total and antral follicle counts, normalized levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, anti-Müllerian hormone, and estradiol, and enhanced yield of metaphase II oocytes. Oocyte quality improved, evidenced by higher mitochondrial membrane potential, increased mitochondrial DNA copy number, and reduced reactive oxygen species levels. scRNA-seq analysis indicated that UCMSCs primarily targeted granulosa and stromal cells, upregulating oxidative phosphorylation pathways and downregulating aging-related pathways (e.g. , p53, mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, Wnt). Notably, the anti-aging gene Klotho was significantly upregulated. Cell communication analysis revealed a reduction in inflammatory signaling (e.g. , transforming growth factor-β), and pseudotime analysis suggested that UCMSCs redirected GC fate away from a pro-inflammatory state. CONCLUSION UCMSCs mitigate ovarian aging by enhancing mitochondrial function, upregulating Klotho, remodeling intercellular communication, and influencing GC fate. These findings offer mechanistic insights into MSC-based therapies for age-related ovarian decline.

article.title: Ramelteon suppresses astrocytic senescence via MT1-cAMP axis to protect dopaminergic neurons
article.authors: Chao Gu; Yajing Chen; Xiaohuan Du; Fang Li; Shuwei Yuan; Wenjing Wang; Ping Guo; Shikai Wang; Mei Wang
article.abstract: Introduction Astrocytic senescence is increasingly recognized as a critical contributor to the pathogenesis of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Ramelteon, a clinically approved MT1/MT2 melatonin receptor agonist, has demonstrated neuroprotective effects in various neurological disorders. However, whether Ramelteon can inhibit astrocytic senescence and the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Methods An in vivo MPTP-induced mouse model of PD was used to evaluate the therapeutic potential of Ramelteon. An in vitro long-term culture-induced replicative senescence model (40 days in vitro , DIV) and MPP + -induced premature senescence model in primary astrocytes were employed. Immunoblotting, real-time quantitative PCR, immunofluorescence, SA-β-gal staining, and immunohistochemistry were performed to assess astrocytic senescence, dopaminergic neuronal survival, and motor function. Results Ramelteon treatment significantly attenuated MPTP-induced dopaminergic neuronal loss in the substantia nigra compacta (SNc) and improved motor deficits in mice. In vitro , Ramelteon markedly suppressed both replicative and MPP + -induced astrocytic senescence, as evidenced by decreased p16 Ink4a and SA-β-gal activity, restored LaminB1 expression, and reduced senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors ( IL-6 , IL-1β , CXCL10 , and MMP9 ). Mechanistically, knockdown of Mtnr1a (encoding MT1), but not Mtnr1b (encoding MT2), largely abolished the anti-senescence effects of Ramelteon. MT1 activation inhibited adenylate cyclase (AC) activity and reduced intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. Notably, senescent astrocytes exhibited elevated cAMP levels, and the cAMP inhibitor SQ22536 mimicked while the cAMP analog dbcAMP reversed the anti-senescence effects of Ramelteon. Furthermore, Ramelteon reduced mitochondrial ROS (mitoROS) production in senescent astrocytes through MT1-cAMP signaling. Discussion Our findings demonstrate that Ramelteon inhibits astrocytic senescence through MT1 receptor-mediated cAMP suppression and mitochondrial ROS reduction, thereby protecting DA neurons in a PD mouse model. This study identifies Ramelteon as a potential therapeutic agent for PD by suppressing astrocytic senescence through MT1 activation.

article.title: White matter hyperintensities and amyloid pathology in cognitively unimpaired aging: topographical, microstructural, and network-level evidence
article.authors: Sana Mohammadi; Minoo Sharbafshaaer; Maria Agnese Pirozzi; Francesca Trojsi; Sadegh Ghaderi; Yasser Iturria-Medina; Seyed-Mohammad Fereshtehnejad
article.abstract: The frequent coexistence of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) and β-amyloid (Aβ) pathology in cognitively unimpaired older adults complicates interpretation of vascular and neurodegenerative imaging findings. This narrative review synthesizes topographical, microstructural, and network-level evidence in cognitively unimpaired aging, distinguishing biomarker-characterized samples from supportive mixed or symptomatic cohorts. WMHs have heterogeneous etiologies. Posterior and some periventricular patterns are associated with cerebral Aβ in several cohorts, but lobar location and distance from the ventricles are overlapping classifications, and vascular associations are not confined to frontal or deep lesions. Independent and additive cognitive associations are more consistently reported than interactions. Longitudinal executive-function interactions reported in a dissertation and related abstract remain preliminary and non-independent. Some longitudinal studies associate baseline Aβ with subsequent WMH accrual, but findings are not uniform and do not establish causation. APOE-related findings vary with age, population, and amyloid burden. Diffusion MRI detects tissue abnormalities beyond visible lesions, although microstructural and disconnectome measures require prospective validation before they can improve individual prognosis. Anti-amyloid trial evidence identifies MRI safety considerations; effects on chronic WMH progression remain uncertain.

article.title: The aging secretome as a candidate driver of bone remodeling imbalance: myokines, adipokines, and senescence-associated secretory factors
article.authors: Hanhong Fang; Xianglong Zhou; Yang Liu; Weicheng Chen; Fulin Zhou; Haoran Zhou; Jianhui Xiang; Liming Xiong
article.abstract: Bone homeostasis depends on the spatial and temporal coupling of osteoclastic resorption to osteoblastic formation. With aging, this balance shifts toward net bone loss alongside sarcopenia, marrow adipose expansion, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These parallel changes may be linked by a shared set of secreted signals, termed here the aging secretome. We distinguish functional remodeling imbalance, defined as a sustained shift between formation and resorption, from direct uncoupling, in which a resorption-to-formation coupling signal is demonstrably disrupted. The aging secretome comprises three principal arms: muscle-derived signals, including myostatin, irisin, and myogenic extracellular vesicles; fat-derived signals, including leptin, adiponectin, and marrow adipocyte lipotoxicity; and senescence-associated secretory factors, particularly those involving senescent osteocytes, TNF-α, and IL-6. Inflammaging is treated as a shared contextual amplifier rather than a separate signaling arm. These pathways converge on key regulators of skeletal remodeling, including RANKL, Wnt–sclerostin, and IGF-1. This framework also provides a common context for comparing pathway-specific interventions, such as activin type II receptor blockade and sclerostin inhibition, with broader approaches targeting senescence or inflammation. An early phase 2 senolytic trial was negative overall, with only an exploratory signal in women with high senescent-cell burden. The aging secretome should therefore be viewed as an organizing framework whose individual pathways and relative contributions require further validation in human bone.

article.title: Brain insulin resistance and microglial immunometabolic dysregulation in neurodegenerative diseases
article.authors: Xinyu Liu; Xiaorong Zhang; Yufang Su; Gaopeng Guan; Xianjun Luo; Puhua Zhang
article.abstract: Brain insulin resistance (BIR) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to the development and progression of neurodegenerative diseases rather than simply a metabolic abnormality. In the central nervous system, insulin signaling is involved in neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, energy metabolism, and protein homeostasis. Increasing evidence suggests that impaired brain insulin signaling is associated with Alzheimer disease (AD), Parkinson disease (PD), and other neurodegenerative conditions, although the mechanisms linking BIR to persistent inflammation and neuronal injury remain incompletely understood. Microglia, the principal innate immune cells of the central nervous system, integrate metabolic and immune signals and may therefore provide an important link between impaired insulin signaling and chronic inflammation. BIR may disrupt insulin receptor substrate (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and protein kinase B (Akt) signaling and promote nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired mitophagy, and lysosomal and lipid metabolic disturbances. These changes may promote activation of the NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, inflammatory mediator release, excessive phagocytosis, and synaptic dysfunction. In turn, persistent microglial inflammation may further impair insulin signaling, forming a reciprocal feedback loop that sustains pathological changes. This review summarizes the mechanisms linking BIR to microglial immunometabolic dysfunction and discusses potential therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic and inflammatory pathways in neurodegenerative diseases.

article.title: Focused Ultrasound Followed by Radiofrequency Microneedling with Bacteria-derived Extracellular Vesicle for Melasma and Skin Aging: A Retrospective Case Series
article.authors: Trong Vo
article.abstract: Background : Melasma and facial skin aging are multifactorial conditions involving pigmentary, inflammatory, vascular, and dermal remodeling pathways. Combination energy-based device (EBD) protocols are designed to target multiple pathways in a single treatment course. However, real-world data on focused ultrasound and radiofrequency (RF) microneedling combined with exosome delivery, for managing melasma and facial skin aging are limited. Case Presentation : This is a retrospective, single-center case series of four patients aged 50 to 60 years with Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III to IV, presenting with mixed-type melasma, and facial skin aging. During the first session, each patient received dot-mode focused ultrasound (LinearZ) followed 30 minutes later by monopolar RF microneedling (POTENZA) with 1.5 mL of a bacteria-derived extracellular vesicle solution (RexoFace). Patients subsequently received one or two additional RF microneedling sessions at 6-week intervals. Thus, the interval from baseline to the final 4-week post-treatment assessment was approximately 10 weeks for patients receiving two RF sessions and 16 weeks for the patient receiving three RF sessions. Outcomes were assessed descriptively on standardized clinical photographs and images obtained with the Sylton OBSERV 520x imaging platform at baseline and 4 weeks after the final session. All four patients showed investigator-assessed improvement in melasma pigmentation, skin quality, and clinical signs of facial aging. Assessment was unblinded and no validated severity instrument was applied. Mild to moderate erythema with edema followed each RF microneedling session and decreased without intervention within 45 minutes. No serious adverse events, scarring, infection, or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation were recorded during the 4-week observation period. Since the follow-up was limited to 4 weeks after the final session, these observations do not establish medium-term cutaneous safety or durability. Conclusions : In this retrospective four-patient case series, the combined protocol of dot-mode focused ultrasound and monopolar RF microneedling with a bacteria-derived extracellular vesicle solution was associated with visible improvement and was well tolerated over a short observation period.

article.title: Epigenetic aging in the tumor microenvironment: mechanisms and implications for immunotherapy
article.authors: Fusako Takezawa; Yohei Sato
article.abstract: Aging reshapes the tumor microenvironment (TME) by altering the immune, stromal, and vascular compartments, yet these changes are not fully explained by chronological age. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, and non-coding RNA programs, may contribute to persistent alterations in cellular function and communication. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on epigenetic remodeling in the aged TME, distinguishing established findings in aging and cancer from mechanisms that remain to be demonstrated specifically in aged tumors. We highlight how epigenetic changes intersect with cellular senescence, chronic inflammation, and metabolic stress to weaken antitumor immunity and influence treatment response, with particular attention to T-cell dysfunction, regulatory T-cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. We also discuss the limitations of bulk-tissue epigenetic clocks and the emerging value of cell-resolved and spatial analyses. Finally, we consider therapeutic implications, including epigenetic therapies, senescence-directed interventions, and selective targeting of suppressive immune-stromal interactions, while noting that their ability to reverse TME aging remains uncertain. Integrating longitudinal human studies with functional experiments will be essential to determine whether epigenetically altered immune-stromal niches can serve as biomarkers or therapeutic targets beyond chronological age alone.

article.title: Maintaining Klotho: preventing the body from unwinding
article.authors: Walter H. Gunzburg; Pharon Pawa; Brian Salmons
article.abstract: The Klotho gene, discovered in 1997, encodes a protein that plays a pivotal role in regulating aging and longevity. Reduced Klotho expression is associated with multiple age-related diseases, including renal, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders, leading to the notion that supplementation of the levels of Klotho may have a beneficial, or even a therapeutic, effect. Despite promising early stage results from recombinant and gene-based therapies, clinical translation has been hindered in part by the protein’s short half-life as well as the immune clearance of Klotho producing cells. This article reviews Klotho’s biological significance and therapeutic challenges, as well as introducing a novel encapsulation-based approach—Cell-in-a-Box® technology—as a proposed potential solution for sustained Klotho delivery. Encapsulated Klotho-producing cells may potentially enable continuous secretion, immune protection, and long-term efficacy, offering a transformative strategy for anti-aging and disease modification.

article.title: The Biochemical Landscapes Of Longevity: Interplay Between Mitochhondrial Dysfunction, Nutrient Sensing Pathways, And Metabolic Strategies To Halt Aging
article.authors: Erhan OKTAY
article.venue: International Journal of Medical Science and Public Health Research
article.abstract: Aging is characterized by a progressive decline in physiological integrity, leading to impaired cellular function and increased vulnerability to metabolic, neurodegenerative, and cardiovascular diseases. In the field of medical biochemistry, aging is no longer viewed as a passive, entropic process but rather as a highly regulated biological phenomenon governed by interconnected molecular pathways. This academic review aims to analyze the intricate biochemical interplay between mitochondrial dysfunction and nutrient-sensing networks during cellular senescence, while critically evaluating the efficacy of current metabolic interventions designed to preserve healthspan and extend human longevity. A systematic literature search was conducted across the PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases for peer-reviewed studies, clinical cohort analyses, and systematic reviews published up to October 2026. Search strings combined core biochemical keywords including "human longevity", "mitochondrial dysfunction", "nutrient-sensing pathways", "Sirtuins", "mTORC1", and "NAD+ boosters". Prioritization was given to multi-omics studies, clinical trials, and geroscience frameworks validated in human plasma, serum, or non-human primate models. Studies tracking macrovascular pathologies without clear aging biomarker endpoints were excluded. The biochemical hallmarks of aging are centered around a state of cellular energy crisis and dysregulated nutrient signaling. Mitochondria, the main hubs of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) generation via oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), experience a marked functional decline with age. This is driven by the accumulation of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, loss of membrane potential, and a failure in selective macroautophagy (mitophagy). The resulting mitochondrial collapse drastically increases the production of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), triggering cellular stress responses and the chronic, sterile inflammation known as "inflammaging." Simultaneously, nutrient-sensing networks undergo pathological shifts. The continuous, hyperactivation of the Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1)-driven by nutrient-rich diets-suppresses cytoprotective autophagy and accelerates cellular senescence. Conversely, critical energy sensors such as Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase (AMPK) and the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent Sirtuins (SIRT1-7) exhibit severe systemic depletion. The age-dependent drop in the NAD+/NADH ratio impairs the activation of the rate-limiting salvage enzyme Nicotinamide Phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), paralyzing nuclear-mitochondrial communication. To counteract these transformations, advanced metabolic interventions show great therapeutic potential. Administering exogenous NAD+ precursors, such as Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) or Nicotinamide Riboside (NR), successfully restores the NAD+ pool, re-activating SIRT1 and SIRT6 to improve insulin sensitivity and mitigate epigenetic biological aging. Furthermore, lifestyle interventions—including dietary amino acid restriction and intermittent fasting—activate the stress-response transcription factor ATF4, downregulate mTORC1, and promote mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1alpha. Human longevity is dynamically dictated by the functional synchronization of mitochondrial health and nutrient-sensing pathways. Transitioning clinical focus toward multi-analyte biochemical profiling—quantifying plasma NAD+ availability, sirtuin enzyme kinetics, and circulating epigenetic methylation markers—provides a non-invasive strategy to measure biological age and design precise geroscience interventions capable of halting metabolic degeneration.

article.title: Triterpenoids – future multi-target compounds against obesity and towards restoration of metabolic health
article.authors: Johanna Becker; Birgitta E. Ebert; Gunter Festel; Lars M. Blank
article.abstract: Obesity and its associated diseases represent one of the most urgent public health crises of our time, affecting billions worldwide. Current pharmacological agents, such as GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, have demonstrated high clinical efficacy in diabetes and weight management. However, the required lifelong medication is often limited by high economic costs and severe side effects, including gastrointestinal complications. Consequently, the search for complementary therapies is invaluable. This review highlights the potential of natural triterpenoids in obesity management by shifting the focus towards long-term metabolic restoration. Triterpenoids can serve as multi-target agents that address key pathways, such as AMPK and Akt/mTOR, thereby positively regulating autophagy processes and improving metabolic imbalances. Celastrol, for example, acts as a leptin sensitizer, restoring satiety signaling; ursolic acid drives body recomposition by enhancing energy expenditure; and ginsenosides modulate multiple processes, including browning, adipogenesis, lipogenesis, and satiety signaling. Furthermore, oleanolic acid promotes pathways associated with cellular healthspan by activating telomerase, while betulinic acid suppresses de novo fatty acid synthesis independently of food intake. However, low oral bioavailability remains the major challenge to successfully translating these findings from animal models to clinical applications. Advanced strategies, such as sustainable bioproduction via genetically modified microorganisms, engineered probiotics, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems, offer promising opportunities to overcome these pharmacokinetic and safety limitations. Addressing these barriers is essential to translate triterpenoids into therapeutic agents for human metabolic health and healthy aging.

article.title: Effects of Environmental Aging Pathways on the Formation, Composition and Settling Behavior of Microplastic–Oil Agglomerates
article.authors: Yue Yu; Wanran Li; Sinian Jin; Moran Ju; Qing Su
article.abstract: Marine oil spills and microplastic (MP) pollution frequently coexist, but the effects of microplastic aging on microplastic–oil agglomerates’ (MOAs) formation and transport remain poorly resolved. In this study, polybutylene terephthalate and polyvinyl chloride microplastics were subjected to acid, UV, and sequential UV→Acid aging and then interacted with three crude oils under controlled mixing conditions. Surface properties were related to oil dispersion efficiency, MOA size, composition, and settling behavior. Aging generated pathway-specific surface states rather than a single monotonic weathering trend. Acid aging increased negative surface charge and wettability, coinciding with reduced oil capture and smaller MP-enriched aggregates. UV aging caused surface roughening and was associated with larger, more MP-rich aggregates, consistent with a greater contribution of MP-MP contacts despite reduced hydrophobic affinity. Sequential UV→Acid aging combined more negative charge, increased roughness and elevated surface free energy. These MPs formed large, MP-rich MOAs with relatively high settling velocities despite reduced oil affinity. Aggregate size became decoupled from captured oil mass after aging, while relatively high oil dispersion could coexist with rapid MOA settling. These findings indicate the potential for partial separation of petroleum-hydrocarbon and MP transport and highlight the importance of aging pathway, polymer chemistry, and aggregate composition.

article.title: Functional Deficits and Diffusion Tensor Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Olfactory and Vision Systems in the Alzheimer’s Disease Model of Aging GluN3A Knockout Mice
article.authors: Ling Wei; Michael Qize Jiang; Yingying Zhao; Daiana Takashima; Yi Li; Khan Hekmatyar; Lingyue Wu; Ananth Sastry; Jenny J. Yang; Shan Ping Yu
article.abstract: Sensory dysfunction, such as olfactory and visual deficits, is a notorious symptom during the progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and related dementia (ADRD). The causal factor/s and structural disruptions underlying the sensory dysfunction in the AD/ADRD brain are not well understood. The NMDA receptor subunit GluN3A (NR3A) negatively regulates the receptor activity to uphold cellular Ca2+ homeostasis. In GluN3A knockout (KO) mice, animals spontaneously develop chronic neurodegenerative excitotoxicity, cognitive decline, and AD-like pathology. Using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), we examined neuronal network destruction together with sensory dysfunction in the GluN3A KO mouse. Specific attention was given to the selective vulnerability of the olfactory and visual nuclei, white matter injury in regional connections between subcortical centers and the cortex and hippocampus. Compared to age-matched wild-type (WT) controls (male), consistent with our early reports in younger ages, 18-month-old aging/aged GluN3A KO mice (male) suffered significant olfactory, visual and social deficits, accompanied by marked Aβ42 deposition in the brain. Ex vivo MR images of the GluN3A KO and control brains were acquired on the 7T MRI system, using a four-channel mouse array RF coil. High-resolution 3D T2-weighted RARE anatomical and DTI scans were performed. The DTI analysis revealed that GluN3A KO mice developed brain atrophy, involving significant damage in the white and gray matter of the olfactory and visual systems and impaired pathways among the superior colliculus, lateral geniculate nucleus, and the hippocampus and/or the cortex. This investigation disclosed a receptor-mediated neurodegeneration that explains sensory syndromes featured in a sporadic AD mouse model.

article.title: Acute Effects of Exhaustive Exercise on the Anti-Aging Protein S-Klotho in Young Females and Males with Obesity
article.authors: Michael Svensson; Lisa Blomqvist; Torbjörn Åkerfeldt; Pär Steneberg; Christer Malm
article.abstract: Background: Circulating S-Klotho is increasingly recognized as an anti-aging protein linked to cardiovascular protection and metabolic regulation. Although exercise elevates S-Klotho, the dose–response threshold and metabolic determinants of this response in young adults with obesity, a population at heightened risk for cardiometabolic dysfunction, remain poorly characterized. To examine the acute effects of submaximal and maximal cycling on circulating S-Klotho in young adults with obesity and to identify key metabolic predictors of exercise-induced changes. Methods: Eighteen young (26 ± 3 years, BMI 30 ± 2 kg/m2) males and females completed incremental cycling to exhaustion. Serum S-Klotho was assessed at rest, after submaximal (SubMax), and post-maximal (Max) exercise. Covariates included cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max), iDXA body composition, HOMA-IR, and hsCRP. Predictor Screening and Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression with fivefold cross-validation were used to identify determinants of exercise-induced S-Klotho responses. Results: A significant acute increase in S-Klotho was observed (Main Effect of Time: F(2,32) = 9.4, p = 0.0006). Post hoc analysis revealed an intensity-dependent threshold, with a significant surge occurring only between submaximal and maximal exertion (p = 0.021; Rest to Max: p = 0.0005). No significant sex differences or interactions were observed (p > 0.05). The PLS model explained 74% of the variance in S-Klotho changes, identifying systemic inflammation (Log10[hsCRP]) and visceral adiposity as the primary predictive factors. Conclusions: Exhaustive exercise acutely increases circulating S-Klotho in young adults with obesity, independent of sex. This response is intensity-dependent and primarily driven by baseline metabolic risk factors. S-Klotho may represent an acute exercise-responsive biomarker linked to metabolic health in at-risk populations. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in larger and adequately powered studies.

article.title: Associations between air pollution, accelerated biological aging, and oral inflammatory diseases: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort
article.authors: Hui Zhan; Dong Liu; You Guo; Wei Liu
article.abstract: Background The relationships between air pollution exposure and incident risk of oral inflammatory diseases (OIDs) and roles of accelerated biological aging remain unclear. Methods In 348,247 adults from the UK Biobank, the individual levels of air pollutants, including particulate matter (PM) (PM 2.5 , PM 10 , PM 2.5–10, and PM 2.5 absorbance ), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), nitric oxides (NO x ), and air pollution score (multiple air pollutants exposure), were estimated. The associations between air pollution exposure and incident risk of OIDs were assessed. The mediation roles of the Klemera–Doubal method biological age (KDM-BA) acceleration and the phenotypic age (PhenoAge) acceleration were evaluated. Results During the median follow-up of 16.49 years, a total of 3,967 incident OIDs were documented. Each one standard deviation increment in PM 2.5 , PM 10 , PM 2.5–10, PM 2.5 absorbance , NO 2 , NO x , and air pollution score was significantly associated with 8%, 4%, 3%, 5%, 10%, 8%, and 8% increments in incident risk of OIDs, respectively (all p < 0.05). All air pollutants except PM 2.5–10 were significantly and positively associated with KDM-BA acceleration, and all air pollutants were significantly and positively associated with PhenoAge acceleration (all p < 0.05). KDM-BA acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollution (except PM 2.5–10 ) and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 1.21 to 5.42%. PhenoAge acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollutants and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 8.52 to 16.65%. Conclusion Air pollution may contribute to increased incident risk of OIDs, and premature aging may play an important role in the pathogenic process.

article.title: Gut microbiome and aging-related disorders: mechanistic insights and emerging microbiome-targeted therapies for healthy aging
article.authors: Md Minarul Islam; Gabsik Yang; Ki Sung Kang
article.abstract: Background The human gut harbors a diverse and dense microbial community that maintains metabolic, immune, and intestinal homeostasis through a symbiotic relationship with the host. Aging is a complex biological process that involves alterations in the gut microbiome, including decreased microbial diversity and a decline in beneficial microbiota that produce useful metabolites, which impair intestinal barrier function and enhance chronic low-grade inflammation (inflammaging). Scope This review explores current evidence on the interaction between aging and the gut microbiome, emphasizing its impact on age-associated diseases, such as frailty and sarcopenia, cardiovascular issues, type 2 diabetes, obesity, osteoporosis, and neurodegenerative conditions. It further delves into the distinct microbial profiles of centenarians and evaluates microbiome-targeted interventions, such as dietary approaches, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, fecal microbiota transplants, caloric restriction, intermittent fasting, and pharmaceutical agents, by synthesizing evidence from both human and animal research to emphasize their potential in fostering healthy aging and increased longevity. Key findings Evidence from human and preclinical studies suggests that alterations in the gut microbiome associated with aging facilitate immune dysregulation, metabolic dysfunction, and the progression of various chronic diseases. Whereas, centenarians possess distinctive microbial signatures rich in beneficial metabolites that could promote healthy aging and prolonged life. Additionally, microbiome-targeted interventions have demonstrated promise in enhancing gut microbial diversity and host wellbeing, though their clinical effectiveness needs additional validation. Conclusion The gut microbiome is a potential focus for supporting healthy aging and warding off age-related illnesses. Nonetheless, its significant inter-individual variability emphasizes the necessity for personalized microbiome-based approaches, which require validation through extensive longitudinal studies and properly structured randomized controlled trials to demonstrate causality and verify long-term effectiveness.

article.title: The broccoli derivative sulforaphane extends lifespan by slowing the transcriptional aging clock
article.authors: Christine A. Sedore; Erik Segerdell; Anna L. Coleman-Hulbert; Erik Johnson; Jonathan N. Levi; Gordon J. Lithgow; Monica Driscoll; Patrick C. Phillips
article.abstract: Sulforaphane, an organosulfur isothiocyanate derived from cruciferous vegetables, has been shown to inhibit inflammation, oxidative stress, and cancer cell growth. To explore the potential of sulforaphane as a candidate natural compound for promoting longevity more generally, we tested the dose and age-specific effects of sulforaphane on C. elegans longevity, finding that it can extend lifespan by more than 50% at the most efficacious doses, but that treatment must be initiated early in life to be effective. We then created a novel, gene-specific transcriptional aging clock, which demonstrated that sulforaphane-treated individuals exhibited a “transcriptional age” that was approximately four days younger than age-matched controls, representing a nearly 20% reduction in biological age. The clearest transcriptional responses were detoxification pathways, which, together with the shape of the dose-response curve, indicates a likely hormetic response to sulforaphane, which we show are regulated by both the daf-16 /FOXO and skn-1 /Nrf2 transcription factors. These results support the idea that robust longevity-extending interventions can act via global effects across the organism, as revealed by systems level changes in gene expression.

article.title: Os “novos velhos” e os capitais para “envelhecer bem” nos discursos publicitários de Nutren Senior The “new old” and the capitals for “aging well” in Nutren Senior’s advertising discourses Los “nuevos viejos” y los capitales para “envejecer bien” en los discursos publicitarios de Nutren Senior
article.authors: Juan da Cunha Silva; Francisco Romão Ferreira; Shirley Donizete Prado; Ronaldo Gonçalves de Oliveira
article.abstract: This article analyzes the advertising discourses of the Nutren Senior brand, focusing on the representations of aging and the persuasive strategies aimed at constructing a 'good old age.' Based on the analysis of advertising campaigns broadcast on YouTube, the signs, images, and performances that compose the brand's statements are discussed. The study relies on references from Social and Human Sciences and Health to problematize the symbolic capitals associated with active aging, autonomy, and consumption as a form of care. The findings indicate that Nutren Senior promotes an aestheticization of old age, reinforcing normative models of body and identity, and contributing to the reconfiguration of the social roles of older people in the media-advertising context.

article.title: Aging: Emerging Concepts for Life Insurers
article.authors: Timothy Meagher
article.abstract: Interest in understanding the aging process is on the increase, as population aging has accelerated the burden of chronic disease, while advances in biology suggest that aging may be measurable and, perhaps, modifiable. Tests of biological age are now available, and interventions to slow aging and delay the onset of chronic disease are being evaluated. This article introduces the hallmarks of aging as a framework for understanding the biological processes underlying age-related decline. It then reviews tests of biological age, summarizes interventions to slow aging, and considers their possible ramifications for life insurance medicine.

article.title: Aging remodels progenitor and niche interactions in lung regeneration
article.authors: Fernanda Toscano-Marquez; Angeles Garcia-Vicente; Uriel Camacho-Silverio; Tania Valdivia-Herrera; Mariana Río de la Loza; Elisa Hernández-Xóchihua; Remedios Ramírez; Moises Selman; Annie Pardo; Yair Romero
article.abstract: Introduction Progenitor cells in aged tissues undergo changes in their microenvironment that may impact their functionality during regeneration. Despite recent advances in understanding the role of adult lung progenitors, the impact of aging on these cells remains unclear. Methods To analyze aging modifications, we used aged wild-type mice of 18–24 months old, and Zmpste24 –/– deficient mice, which exhibit an accelerated phenotype. A three-dimensional organoid culture system was employed to assess in vitro regenerative capacity. Additionally, cells were isolated and characterized with senescence and autophagy markers. Results Our findings revealed that lung epithelial cells from aged mice and Zmpste24 –/– mice retain organoid forming potential, maintaining their phenotype and cellular homeostasis through increased autophagy-associated transcriptional response, particularly when co-cultured with young fibroblasts. Moreover, these progenitor cells may exhibit increased susceptibility to mechanical stress with aging potentially associated with reduced nuclear lamins and the Zmpste24 defect. This vulnerability is illustrated by FACS sorting, which can further compromise their regenerative potential. By contrast, cultured fibroblasts from Zmpste24 –/– mice show nuclear defects and acquire a senescent phenotype, characterized by the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) activation and reduced autophagy, which in turn impairs organoid formation. Discussion Our results indicate that, in aging, progenitor cells and their fibroblast niche integrate microenvironmental signals that shape cell-cell interactions essential for lung regeneration.

article.title: Mechanical memory in aging: From adaptive sensing to pathological entrenchment
article.authors: Mingyang Huang; Xiaoyu Ma; Ruiqi Gao; Qichen Miao; Guoqing Wang; Ziyuan Liu; Kun Wang; Ming Luo
article.abstract: Abstract Cells can carry forward information from earlier mechanical environments and not only respond to the cue in front of them. This property, usually described as mechanical memory, is important for aging because many old tissues stiffen, whereas their resident cells become less regenerative and less mechanosensitive. This mismatch suggests that aging changes the handling of mechanical information: how it is sensed, transmitted, stored, and used. Here, we review evidence across cytoskeletal organization, focal adhesions and ion channels, nuclear mechanics, chromatin, biomolecular condensates, and metabolism. We treat epigenetic memory as one durable execution layer within mechanical memory and not as a synonym for the whole process. We then use three failure modes—sensor degradation, conduction blockade, and execution blockade—to organize aging‐related mechanical‐memory failure. This scheme helps explain why similar modules, including YAP/TAZ, the LINC complex, and repressive chromatin marks, have different consequences in skeletal muscle, bone and cartilage, lung, heart, skin, and brain. We also discuss condensate maturation and liquid‐to‐solid transitions as possible consolidation mechanisms, while emphasizing that direct in vivo evidence of normal aging remains limited. Finally, we classify therapeutic ideas by target layer, evidence strength, reversibility, and translational risk. The review therefore frames mechanical memory as a multilayer, tissue‐dependent process that may help explain why physical history contributes to degeneration with age.

article.title: Transcriptomics Reveals Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes Activate Hepatocyte Longevity-Regulating Pathway in Acute-On-Chronic Liver Failure
article.authors: Deng-na Lin; Yong-qi Zhang; Hai-xia Sun; Yang Li; Wen-yu Li; Jing Zhang; Xiao-hua Yang; Xiang Gao
article.abstract: Background: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), a rapidly progressive condition with high short-term mortality in patients with chronic liver disease, has shown therapeutic responsiveness to mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (MSC-exos) in preclinical studies, where exosome administration significantly attenuates hepatic injury. To comprehensively delineate the mechanistic basis of this therapeutic effect, we conducted integrated miRNA and mRNA sequencing analyses on liver tissues obtained from exosome-treated ACLF murine models. Methods: Mice subjected to a CCl4-based acute-on-chronic liver injury regimen received saline or an MSC-derived extracellular vesicle (EV) preparation intravenously through the tail vein. Liver miRNA and mRNA profiles were examined by differential expression, GSEA, functional enrichment, exploratory LASSO feature selection and integrative network analysis. Expression measurements were complemented by senescence-associated transcript assays, a Cat 3′UTR reporter assay and CCK-8 assessment in cell models. Results: Exosome treatment significantly activated longevity-regulating pathways, mitophagy, and glutathione metabolism in ACLF mice, concurrent with characteristic remodeling of hepatic immune infiltration involving follicular helper T cells, activated NK cells, and macrophage subpopulations. Hepatic injury severity demonstrated positive correlations with mmu-let-7j and Mmp27, and negative associations with mmu-let-7f-2-3p and Tmem8b. The reconstructed miRNA-mRNA network converged on FoxO signaling-mediated regulation of oxidative stress, cellular senescence and autophagy, with FoxO/Catalase (Cat) identified as core regulators. Experimental studies confirmed that MSC-derived exosomes downregulated miR-7b-5p in hepatocytes and enhanced Cat expression, with attenuation of cellular senescence. Conclusions: Integrative transcriptomic analysis revealed that MSC-exos activate the FoxO/Cat axis through miRNA-mRNA interactome remodeling, thereby orchestrating coordinated antioxidant, pro-autophagic, and anti-senescence effects alongside immune microenvironment reprogramming in liver failure. These findings establish a pivotal theoretical framework for developing exosome-based therapeutic strategies targeting hepatic disorders.

article.title: Dentin Collagen Crosslinking for Enhanced Resin–Dentin Bond Longevity: Evidence and Clinical Perspectives
article.authors: Reem A. Ajaj
article.abstract: Abstract The durability of the dentin–resin bonded interface remains a major challenge in adhesive dentistry, largely due to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of exposed collagen fibrils within the hybrid layer. Endogenous proteolytic enzymes, particularly matrix metalloproteinases and cysteine cathepsins, play a critical role in the progressive degradation of the exposed collagen matrix. Collagen crosslinking has emerged as a promising strategy to stabilize the dentin matrix, enhance resistance to endogenous proteases, and potentially improve the long-term durability of adhesive bonds; however, current evidence remains largely experimental, and its routine clinical application is still limited. This narrative review synthesizes current preclinical and emerging translational evidence on collagen crosslinking approaches investigated to reinforce the dentin–resin interface and the characterization techniques used to evaluate their effectiveness. Emphasis is placed on mechanisms of action, key evaluation approaches, and potential clinical relevance. While several crosslinking strategies, particularly carbodiimide-based systems and polyphenol-derived agents, demonstrate encouraging in vitro and laboratory-based outcomes, significant barriers to routine clinical translation persist. These include application time, penetration depth, esthetic concerns, biocompatibility, and integration within existing clinical adhesive workflows. Future research should prioritize clinically feasible formulations, standardized testing protocols, and long-term in vivo and clinical validation to facilitate the potential translation of collagen crosslinking strategies into clinically durable adhesive restorations.

article.title: Histone lactylation mediates the regulation of dental follicle cells' senescence driven by RUNX2 during the process of tooth eruption
article.authors: Lingli Ji; Weiwei Zhao; Jie Li; Dandan Liu; Chenying Zhang; Xiaozhe Wang; Yang Liu; Shuguo Zheng
article.abstract: Abstract Cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD), an autosomal dominant disorder caused by RUNX2 mutation, is characterized by delayed or failed eruption of the permanent teeth; however, the pathogenesis of tooth impaction remains unclear. Tooth eruption is a complex developmental process in which the dental follicle plays a crucial role. Although the dental follicle is known to coordinate osteoclastogenesis and osteogenesis, the precise cellular mechanisms that initiate eruption are still not fully defined. Moreover, how dental follicles activate the signals of tooth eruption and whether the other biological alterations occur in CCD dental follicles have not been reported. Previous work from our group demonstrated that RUNX2 mutations inhibit dental follicle cell senescence in CCD patients. Cellular senescence participates in diverse physiological and pathological processes and is increasingly implicated as a dynamic regulator of morphogenesis and tissue remodeling. This study investigates whether the senescence of dental follicle cells (DFCs) critically mediates tooth eruption and elucidates its underlying regulatory mechanism. Analysis of dental follicle tissues showed a significant reduction in SA-β-gal-positive and P16 INK4a -positive cells in CCD patients compared with healthy controls. Animal studies revealed a progressive accumulation of senescent cells in the dental follicle during normal tooth eruption, whereas this accumulation was suppressed in Runx2 +/− mice, which exhibit delayed tooth eruption. Inhibition of dental follicle senescence via nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) in wild-type mice similarly delayed tooth eruption, confirming the functional necessity of DFCs senescence. Mechanistically, RUNX2 knockdown or mutation upregulated HDAC3 expression, which catalyzed histone delactylation, predominantly at H3K18. The reduced H3K18la levels could lead to transcriptional repression of PLAU. Thus, RUNX2 knockdown or mutation suppressed DFCs senescence via the HDAC3/H3K18la/PLAU axis. Collectively, our study reveals that DFCs senescence acts as an important driver of tooth eruption and identifies a novel epigenetic regulatory mechanism involving histone lactylation that regulates cellular senescence mediated by RUNX2.

article.title: SA-β-Gal stratification reveals senescence-associated heterogeneity and differential cell death susceptibility in human CD8 effector T cells
article.authors: Luis Garza-Martínez; Mark Apadeer; Nica Mariz Aquino; Paolo S. Turano; Elizabeth Akbulut; Dillon Oswald; Sukhwinder Singh; Patricia Fitzgerald-Bocarsly
article.abstract: Introduction Cellular senescence in human T cells remains incompletely defined, particularly with respect to how senescence-associated states influence susceptibility to cell death. Methods We used flow-cytometric SPiDER-based detection of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) activity to profile human CD8+ T-cell subsets from young and old donors. We stratified effector memory (CD8 EM ) and effector memory re-expressing CD45RA (CD8 EMRA ) subsets by the lowest (bottom 25%) and highest (top 25%) quartiles of SA-β-Gal signal. Results CD8 EM and CD8 EMRA cells displayed the greatest within-subset heterogeneity in SA-β-Gal activity. The SA-β-Gal low and high populations occupied distinct regions in UMAP projections and were reproducibly enriched in different FlowSOM metaclusters, indicating that SA-β-Gal activity captures structured phenotypic states within differentiated CD8+ T-cell compartments. These states differed in senescence-associated markers, including CD27, CD28, CD57, and CX3CR1, as well as granzyme-associated programs involving Gzm A, B and K, whereas chronological age had only a limited effect once subsets were analyzed separately. Functionally, nutrient-limited conditions unmasked marked differences in cell death susceptibility between these populations. Following PMA/ionomycin stimulation, SA-β-Gal high CD8 EM and CD8 EMRA cells underwent accelerated stimulation-induced cell death, showed increased caspase-3/7 activation, and exhibited lower post-treatment γH2AX signal relative to SA-β-Gal low counterparts. In contrast, in the absence of stimulation-induced energetic demand, SA-β-Gal high cells displayed greater resistance to cell death. Discussion Together, SA-β-Gal stratification resolves structured heterogeneity within human CD8 effector T cells and supports a context-dependent model in which senescence-associated effector states become selectively vulnerable to stimulation-induced death under metabolic stress.

article.title: Cellular senescence in ovarian cancer: context-dependent effects on tumor immunity and therapy response
article.authors: Yubo Zhang; Mengqi Deng; Junyi Jiang
article.abstract: Cellular senescence is a stress-responsive state marked by sustained proliferative arrest and changes in metabolism, chromatin organization, secretion, and immune signaling. In ovarian cancer (OC), platinum therapy and PARP inhibition can generate senescence-associated states with distinct consequences. Their effects depend on treatment context, cellular compartment, stability of arrest, and the surrounding immune state. Therapy-induced senescent tumor cells may increase antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling and, in immune-competent settings, facilitate dendritic-cell and CD8+ T-cell responses. Persistent senescence can instead maintain a SASP that remodels stromal and immune compartments and may support residual disease, dissemination, or relapse. OC studies have linked altered senescence responses to cisplatin resistance, while senescence-associated states have also been reported after PARP inhibition and taxane treatment. Senescence in CAFs, mesothelial cells, adipose-associated stroma, and immune cells can further alter tumor-cell survival, invasion, immune surveillance, and treatment response. We therefore distinguish stable TIS from reversible senescence-like or dormant states and separate tumor-cell effects from stromal and immune effects. Senolysis, SASP modulation, ferroptosis, and immune-mediated clearance represent potential strategies, but most evidence remains preclinical. Overall, senescence in OC is best viewed as a context-dependent state that can either support antitumor immunity or facilitate immune escape and treatment persistence.

article.title: Plant-Derived Bioactive Compounds, Cancer Stemness and Cellular Senescence: A Narrative Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Relevance to Cancer Recurrence and Drug Resistance
article.authors: Sara Naseer; Wai-Yann Tan; Yin-Teng Sow; Zhi-Yin Wai; Sahana-Shri Ramanitharan; Paey-Ern Bay; Ching-Hsein Chen; Soi-Moi Chye
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cancer recurrence and drug resistance arise from tumour-cell plasticity and microenvironmental adaptations that may persist after treatment. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are associated with self-renewal, tumour initiation, residual disease, and treatment tolerance, whereas cellular senescence has context-dependent effects. Although therapy-induced senescence may restrict tumour-cell proliferation, persistent senescent tumour or stromal cells and their senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can, in selected models, promote inflammatory signalling, stemness-associated phenotypes and therapeutic resistance. This narrative review critically evaluates preclinical and translational evidence concerning curcumin, resveratrol, epigallocatechin gallate, berberine, piperine and shikonin as potential adjunctive modulators of CSCs and senescence-associated processes. Methods: Relevant literature was identified through searches of the MEDLINE/PubMed database from June 2000 and July 2026, using terms related to plant-derived bioactive compounds, CSCs, cellular senescence, SASP, recurrence and drug resistance. Evidence was evaluated according to model relevance, exposure, functional validation and whether it represented direct cross-axis evidence, intermediate mechanistic evidence, or marker- and pathway-level support. Results: Most studies examined CSCs and senescence as separate processes. Direct evidence showing that the same compound, within the same cancer model, modifies a validated cancer stem-cell function and a defined senescence or SASP and subsequently reduces resistance or recurrence is limited or absent. Moreover, poor bioavailability, variable formulations, potentially unachievable experimental exposures, drug interactions, tumour heterogeneity and limited clinical evidence constrain translation. Conclusions: Future studies should incorporate pharmacologically relevant exposures, functional and longitudinal endpoints, causal validation and biomarker-guided combination designs to determine whether these compounds can safely complement standard anticancer therapies.

article.title: Therapeutic induction of Nrf2 activation to reduce senescence in COPD
article.authors: Inés Roger; Paula Montero; Cristina Estornut; Maria Anton; Carolina Ferrer-Gomez; Ángel Cogolludo; Juan Escrivá; Julio Cortijo; Javier Milara
article.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a disease of accelerated lung aging, characterized by oxidative stress, persistent inflammation, and accumulation of senescent cells. Impaired activity of the antioxidant regulator nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) contributes to redox imbalance in COPD; however, whether pharmacological activation of Nrf2 can directly modulate senescence-associated processes in COPD remains unclear. Methods We first analyzed senescence markers in lung tissue from COPD patients across GOLD stages. We then investigated the effects of pharmacological Nrf2 activation using obacunone, omaveloxolone, and the reference compound bardoxolone, with metformin as a senescence-modulating comparator, in primary human bronchial epithelial cells (HBECs) from control subjects and COPD patients exposed to cigarette smoke extract (CSE). Senescence hallmarks, including oxidative stress, DNA damage, cell-cycle arrest, and SASP mediators, were assessed. Translational relevance was further evaluated in a murine model of acute lung injury–induced senescence. Results COPD lung tissue exhibited increased DNA damage, altered senescence markers, and telomere shortening, which correlated with disease severity. In HBECs, CSE induced oxidative stress, Nrf2 activation, DNA damage, senescence markers, and SASP factor release, with more pronounced effects in COPD-derived cells. Pharmacological Nrf2 activators significantly enhanced antioxidant defenses, reduced γH2AX accumulation, attenuated senescence markers (p21, p16, SA-β-gal), and suppressed IL-1β and IL-6 secretion in both control and COPD HBECs. Obacunone showed the most consistent protective profile. These effects were recapitulated in vivo, where Nrf2 activation mitigated inflammation, tissue remodeling, and senescence-associated alterations. Conclusions This study demonstrates that pharmacological activation of Nrf2 restores senescence-associated alterations in both healthy and COPD airway epithelial cells and in an in vivo model of lung injury–induced senescence. These findings identify Nrf2 activation, particularly via obacunone, as a promising strategy to target senescence-driven lung pathology.

article.title: Drought‐induced leaf senescence and regreening upon rewatering associated with chlorophyll metabolism in Kentucky bluegrass
article.authors: Devan Gladden; Stephanie Rossi; Bingru Huang
article.abstract: Abstract Drought stress is a major factor limiting the quality and persistence of cool‐season turfgrass species by accelerating leaf senescence and reducing overall vigor. This study was conducted to examine physiological responses associated with drought‐induced leaf senescence and post‐drought regreening in Kentucky bluegrass ( Poa pratensis L.), with particular emphasis on chlorophyll metabolism. Plants of two cultivars, Baron and Bewitched, were grown under controlled environmental conditions and subjected to well‐watered control and drought stress treatments, with post‐drought rewatering. Physiological parameters such as turf quality, relative water content, chlorophyll fluorescence, and chlorophyll content were evaluated throughout drought and recovery. In addition, the activities of a chlorophyll degradation enzyme, pheophytinase (PPH), and a chlorophyll synthesis enzyme, porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), were measured in response to drought and rewatering to observe the effect of drought on chlorophyll metabolism and to determine which pathway plays a more important role. Drought stress caused leaf dehydration, chlorophyll loss, reduced photochemical efficiency, and lower turf quality in both cultivars, although these parameters recovered following rewatering. PPH activity increased significantly during prolonged drought stress, whereas PBGD activity did not change significantly under drought. During post‐drought recovery, PBGD activity increased, while PPH activity declined to non‐stress levels. The decline in chlorophyll during drought‐induced leaf senescence may be associated with enhanced chlorophyll degradation enzyme activity, whereas the regreening observed during rewatering is likely related to the resumption of chlorophyll synthesis. These findings provide insight into the physiological mechanisms controlling drought‐induced senescence and post‐stress recovery in turfgrass and may be useful for the development of drought‐tolerant cultivars.

article.title: Kanzan cherry blossom and its active compounds attenuate methylglyoxal-induced skin fibroblast senescence through RAGE/NF-κB suppression and ECM restoration
article.authors: Limin Ouyang; Huiji Zhou; Binrui Yang; Xue Zhang; Xuefei Cai; Jiawei Zhang; Bo Li; Liang Chen
article.abstract: Introduction The accumulation of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) is a key driver of skin aging, accelerating the process through oxidative stress, inflammation, and disruption of extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis. Cerasus serrulata 'Sekiyama' Kanzan cherry blossom (KCB) is rich in bioactive compounds with antioxidant and anti-glycation potential. However, its compositional variations across flowering stages and their functional relevance remain unclear. Methods This study systematically characterized the chemical profile of KCB using UPLC-QTOF-MS and monitored six major active components across four flowering stages using UPLC-MS/MS. The anti-glycation, antioxidant, tyrosinase, and collagenase activities of the identified compounds were evaluated in vitro . The protective effects of KCB extract (KCBE) and major active compounds were further investigated in a methylglyoxal (MGO)-induced human skin fibroblast senescence model. Results Thirteen compounds were identified, including one organic acid, five flavonoid glycosides, and seven phenolic acids. The half-bloom stage (KCB3) contained the highest levels of the six quantified compounds. 1- O -caffeoyl glucoside (CG) was the predominant phenolic acid (8.025 ± 0.203%), while quercetin 3- O -6 ′′ - O -malonyl-β-glucopyranoside (QMG) was the major flavonoid (1.155 ± 0.035%). QMG showed strong anti-glycation activity (IC50 = 0.41 ± 0.01 mM), whereas CG exhibited strong tyrosinase (IC 50 = 0.19 ± 0.03 mM) and collagenase inhibition (IC 50 = 2.51 ± 0.90 mM). KCBE, QMG, and CG significantly alleviated MGO-induced cellular senescence, reduced intracellular ROS, restored F-actin organization, and promoted type I collagen deposition. These effects were associated with suppression of RAGE/NF-κB signaling, normalization of the Nrf2/HO-1-mediated antioxidant response, and restoration of ECM-related gene expression. Discussion Half-bloom KCB exhibits prominent anti-glycation and anti-skin-aging activities, with CG and QMG representing major bioactive constituents.
