Results demonstrate the metabolic versatility of DPA in salmon hepatocytes and highlight the capacity of stable isotope-assisted LC-MS to resolve complex fatty acid pathways, including downstream mediator biosynthesis. This analytical workflow provides a powerful framework for investigating the contributions of dietary DPA, or other fatty acids, to n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid pools and specialized pro-resolving mediators in fish.

article.title: Transcriptional Profiling Links LNC_501 to Cucumber Responses to Fusarium Wilt and Reveals Fatty‐Acid‐Metabolism Changes in Host and Pathogen
article.authors: Cui Haonan; Ding Zhuo; Wang Shuai; Sun Chengzhen
article.abstract: ABSTRACT Fusarium wilt is a devastating soil‐borne disease that severely limits cucumber production. However, the roles of long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in cucumber resistance and the transcriptional interplay between cucumber roots and Foc during infection remain poorly understood. Here, we employed dual RNA‐seq to simultaneously profile cucumber mRNAs, lncRNAs, and Foc transcripts in the roots of resistant and susceptible cucumber lines during the early stages of infection. Comparative transcriptome analysis revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming in both host and pathogen and highlighted cell wall‐related and fatty acid metabolism‐related processes among the major responses associated with the cucumber– Foc interaction. Functional analyses in transgenic cucumber lines further supported LNC_501 as a putative negative regulator associated with resistance to Fusarium wilt. LNC_501 expression was inversely associated with that of a nearby glycine‐rich cell wall structural protein gene, CsGRP1.8 , and altered LNC_501 expression in transgenic plants was accompanied by opposite changes in CsGRP1.8 transcript abundance, suggesting a possible role for lncRNA‐associated cell wall regulation in cucumber defense. In addition, fatty acid metabolism‐related genes in both cucumber and Foc exhibited dynamic and host genotype‐dependent expression patterns during infection, suggesting that fatty acid metabolism may be an important shared component of the cucumber– Foc interaction. Together, these findings identify LNC_501 as a candidate lncRNA associated with cucumber responses to Fusarium wilt and suggest a possible link between LNC_501 , CsGRP1.8 , and cell wall‐related defense. They also highlight coordinated fatty acid metabolism changes in both cucumber and Foc during infection, providing a framework for future mechanistic studies of host–pathogen interaction.

article.title: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) mediated gut breast crosstalk in breast cancer: integrative network analysis of molecular signaling, immune infiltration and prognostic biomarkers
article.authors: Tariq Aziz; Layla A. Alahmari; Nawal H. Siddig; Mai M. Almsaud; Fahad Al-Asmari; Huda A. Alqahtani; Rasha Alonaizan; Yolande Sandrine Mengue Ngadena
article.abstract: Introduction Breast cancer is a heterogeneous malignancy in which metabolic dysregulation, immune remodelling, and complex host microbiota interactions contribute to disease progression and therapeutic response. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including acetate, propionate, and butyrate, may act as important molecular mediators linking the gut microbiome to systemic immune and tumor-associated signalling. However, the molecular networks through which SCFA-mediated signalling may influence breast cancer progression and the tumor immune microenvironment remains poorly characterized. This study aimed to investigate the potential regulatory mechanisms underlying the gut-breast axis by integrating SCFA host interaction networks in breast cancer transcriptomic, prognostic, immune infiltration, and drug gene interaction analyses. Methods The SCFA-host interactome was constructed from the combination of HMDB and PubChem data in a protein-protein interaction network. The identification of hub genes was conducted through topological analysis, followed by validation using TCGA-BRCA RNA-seq data, Kaplan-Meier Survival Analysis, TIMER2.0 immune analysis, and DGIdb repurposing analysis. Results The findings indicated that the genes STAT3, HIF1A, and IL6 served as key nodes connecting SCFA signalling and cancer formation. Selected SCFAs, such as propionate, have direct experimental evidence of involvement in the modulation of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway in breast cancer models, while butyrate has been associated with several breast cancer-related signalling and epigenetic mechanisms. Associations were most strongly identified in acetate which was mainly related to metabolic and immune regulatory pathways. This computational analysis did not give a quantitative ranking of the strength of interaction between SCFA and hub genes. In exploratory survival analysis without multiple-testing correction, increased STAT3 and HIF1A expression was associated with unfavourable relapse-free survival. SCFA-associated immune targets showed positive correlations with CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Discussion This study identifies the SCFA-host interactome as an essential regulatory network in breast cancer. Uncovering metabolic and signalling chokepoints such as STAT3 leads to the discovery of new biomarkers for prognosis and drug targets. This highlights the possibility of exploiting the gut-breast axis to increase immune cell penetration.

article.title: The Effect of Total Flavonoid Content of Butterfly Pea Flower Kombucha on Reducing Serum Total Cholesterol Levels in vitro and in vivo in Rats
article.authors: Agus Suprijono; Aries Koes Sundoro; Ariani Hesti Wulan S
article.venue: Journal of Food and Pharmaceutical Sciences
article.abstract: High-cholesterol foods cause metabolic disorders characterized by high cholesterol levels. Butterfly Pea Flower Kombucha, which contains anthocyanins (flavonoids), was obtained by fermenting a mixture of fresh butterfly pea flowers with a SCOBY (Symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast). This study aimed to determine the effect of butterfly pea flower kombucha in reducing total cholesterol. The study began with the production of butterfly pea flower kombucha from 30%, 40%, and 50% fresh butterfly pea flowers fermented with a SCOBY. Total flavonoid levels were determined using visible spectrophotometry with a wavelength of 439.00 nm. Cholesterol levels were determined in vivo by feeding fermented tea to groups of white rats (C-, C+, S1, S2, and S3) for 10 days, after which they were fed lard for 14 days. The results showed that butterfly pea flower kombucha of 30%, 40%, and 50% had a total flavonoid content of 55.75 + 0.656, 84.59 + 1.912, and 154.38 + 0.476 mgQE/100mL. The sample and control could reduce cholesterol by an average of 11.83 + 0.94%, 21.14 + 1.58%, 31.36 + 0.98%, and 32.85 + 1.17%. Statistical tests showed the effect of butterfly pea flower kombucha which can lower cholesterol. This study shows that consuming butterfly pea flower kombucha can reduce cholesterol.

article.title: Investigation of NPC1L1 and NPC2 Protein Levels in Patients with Cholelithiasis: Implications for Cholesterol Transport and Gallbladder Inflammation
article.authors: Hüsnü Çağrı Genç; Hakkı Coşkun; Cemile Zontul; Ayça Taş; Ömer Topcu; Yavuz Siliğ
article.abstract: Cholelithiasis is a common hepatobiliary disorder associated with impaired cholesterol homeostasis and chronic inflammation. Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) and Niemann–Pick C2 (NPC2) are proteins involved in cholesterol transport; however, their roles in the pathogenesis of cholelithiasis remain unclear. This case–control study investigated serum NPC1L1 and NPC2 levels in 44 patients with cholelithiasis and 44 healthy controls. Serum concentrations of NPC1L1 and NPC2 were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Group comparisons, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, Spearman correlation analysis, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Patients with cholelithiasis were significantly older than controls (p<0.001). Serum NPC1L1 levels showed a decreasing trend in patients but did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.060), whereas serum NPC2 levels were significantly higher in patients with cholelithiasis (p=0.019). ROC analysis demonstrated diagnostic performance for NPC2 (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.640, p=0.019), while NPC1L1 did not reach statistical significance (AUC=0.616, p=0.060). A weak negative correlation was observed between NPC1L1 and NPC2 levels (r=−0.221, p=0.038). Multivariable logistic regression analysis indicated that neither NPC1L1 nor NPC2 was independently associated with cholelithiasis, whereas age remained independently associated with cholelithiasis in the adjusted models. These findings suggest that altered NPC1L1 and NPC2 levels may be associated with cholelithiasis. However, the modest discriminatory performance of NPC2 indicates that these findings should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger studies.

article.title: Cholesterol- and Biosurfactant-Stabilized Ethosomes for Betanin: Formulation, Encapsulation and Controlled In Vitro Release
article.authors: Jagoda Chudzińska-Skorupinska; Agata Wawrzyńczak; Agnieszka Feliczak-Guzik
article.abstract: Betanin is a hydrophilic antioxidant with limited physicochemical stability, motivating the development of vesicular carriers to improve its retention and regulate release. This study employed a systematic, stepwise formulation-screening approach to develop and characterize cholesterol-containing ethosomes, including biosurfactant-modified formulations, for betanin encapsulation. The effects of preparation conditions, surfactant type and concentration, cholesterol content, and betanin loading on colloidal properties and storage stability were evaluated. Encapsulation efficiency, loading capacity, and in vitro release were also investigated. Formulations containing 2.5% (w/w) phospholipid, 30% (w/w) ethanol, 10% (w/w) ethylene glycol, 1% (w/w) cholesterol, and 0.625% (w/w) Tween 20 or Tween 20/Mirasoft® SL L60 mixture, prepared by 3 min homogenization, showed the most favorable performance. Betanin incorporation altered vesicle organization, while encapsulation and release strongly depended on surfactant composition and betanin loading. The highest encapsulation efficiency was 87.87 ± 3.22%, whereas the maximum loading capacity was 0.0271 ± 0.0026%. Release was incomplete and composition-dependent, ranging from 5.67 to 34.49% after 90 min at pH 5.8. The limited release indicated formulation-dependent betanin retention, which may favor controlled delivery but could also restrict active-compound availability. As skin permeation and biological safety were not evaluated, the relevance of these findings for dermal delivery remains to be established. Weibull analysis adequately described the nonlinear release profiles. These findings demonstrate that biosurfactant-modified ethosomes are tunable lipid nanocarriers with composition-dependent encapsulation and in vitro release properties.

article.title: Baseline neutrophil-to-HDL cholesterol ratio is associated with subsequent cerebrovascular accident in patients with microscopic polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
article.authors: Jihye Chung; Lucy Eunju Lee; Jang Woo Ha; Oh Chan Kwon; Yong-Beom Park; Sang-Won Lee
article.abstract: OBJECTIVE: A new index, the neutrophil-to-high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol ratio (NHR), has been reported to predict atherosclerosis and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). This study aimed to investigate the clinical utility of baseline NHR in predicting subsequent complications in patients with microscopic polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MPA/GPA). METHODS: Clinical data of 150 patients with MPA/GPA were analysed retrospectively. Baseline demographic data, the Birmingham vasculitis activity score (BVAS), the five-factor score (FFS), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were recorded. All-cause mortality, relapse, end-stage kidney disease, cerebrovascular accident (CVA), and ACS were evaluated as subsequent complications. NHR was calculated using the following formula: neutrophil count (× 1000/mm3) / HDL-cholesterol levels (mg/dL). NHR was analysed both as a continuous variable and using exploratory categorical cut-offs. Death before CVA was treated as a competing event in the cumulative incidence analysis. RESULTS: The median age was 63.5 years (64.0% female). Baseline NHR was significantly correlated with baseline BVAS, ESR, and CRP levels. Of the five subsequent complications, only subsequent CVA demonstrated a significant area under the curve in a receiver operating characteristic curve analysis of baseline NHR. Continuous NHR was not significantly associated with subsequent CVA after adjustment for age and CRP. In complementary exploratory analyses using the cohort-derived cut-off, patients with baseline NHR ≥ 0.17 had a higher frequency of subsequent CVA and a lower CVA-free survival rate than those with baseline NHR < 0.17. The former group also had a higher cumulative incidence of CVA when death before CVA was treated as a competing event. NHR ≥ 0.17 remained significantly associated with subsequent CVA after adjustment for age and CRP. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrated the clinical utility of baseline NHR in predicting subsequent CVA in patients with MPA/GPA. Key Points • Baseline neutrophil-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio was significantly correlated with baseline Birmingham vasculitis activity score, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein levels in patients with microscopic polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis. • Patients with baseline neutrophil-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio ≥0.17 had a significantly higher risk of subsequent cerebrovascular accident and a lower cerebrovascular accident-free survival rate than those with baseline neutrophil-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio <0.17. • Baseline neutrophil-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio ≥0.17 remained independently associated with subsequent cerebrovascular accident after adjustment for age and C-reactive protein.

article.title: Triglycerides, Total Cholesterol, and Body Weight Index Demonstrates High Discriminative Performance for Metabolic Syndrome: A Comparative Study with Established Cardiometabolic and Inflammatory Indices
article.authors: Mehmet Erdem; Tuğba Raika Kıran; Lezan Keskin; Süleyman Caner Karahan
article.abstract: Objective: This research sought to assess the effectiveness of combined inflammatory and cardiometabolic markers, with a particular focus on the triglycerides, total cholesterol, and body weight index (TCBI), in individuals diagnosed with metabolic syndrome (MetS). Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included individuals aged 18-65 years who were admitted to the internal medicine clinic between January 2023 and January 2026. MetS was defined according to NCEP ATP III criteria. Demographic, anthropometric, and laboratory data were obtained from electronic medical records. In addition to routine biochemical and hematological parameters, composite indices including TCBI, TyG, CMI, CRP/HDL, NHR, UHR, NLAR, PIV, HALP, NLR, SIRI, and SII were calculated using standard formulas. Appropriate statistical tests were utilized to compare groups. To evaluate the diagnostic effectiveness of the indices, a ROC curve analysis was performed. Results: Several anthropometric and metabolic parameters differed significantly between groups (p < 0.05). Among the evaluated indices, TCBI, CMI, TyG, CRP/HDL, NHR, and UHR levels were significantly elevated in MetS patients (p < 0.0001), whereas NLAR, PIV, HALP, NLR, SIRI, and SII showed no significant differences (p > 0.05). ROC analysis demonstrated that TCBI had the highest diagnostic performance (AUC: 0.9622, 95% CI: 0.9378 - 0.9865, p < 0.0001), followed by CMI (AUC: 0.9600) and TyG (AUC: 0.9463). CRP/HDL, NHR, and UHR exhibited moderate discriminative ability. Conclusion: TCBI showed strong diagnostic performance in this cohort and demonstrated higher overall discriminative ability compared with the evaluated indices. These findings suggest that TCBI may represent a simple and accessible marker for MetS assessment. However, further studies are required to validate its clinical utility.

article.title: Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Cholesterol Sulfotransferase as Immunomodulatory Agents
article.authors: Lindsay E. Boudreau; Amanda J. Smith; Hyang Yeon Lee; Bidisha Chakraborty; Kyle R. Abo; Kenneth Chen; Satish K. Nair; Paul J. Hergenrother
article.abstract: Abstract Though immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has been a promising advance in cancer treatment, response rates to ICB are low owing to other mechanisms that cancers employ to evade the immune system. SULT2B1b is an enzyme known to produce cholesterol sulfate (CS), an immunosuppressive metabolite that inhibits T-cell migration. Cancers expressing high levels of SULT2B1b thus generate a tumor microenvironment that excludes T cells, which leads to increased tumor growth and renders ICB therapy ineffective. Here, we identify a novel class of azasteroid SULT2B1b inhibitors with greater potency and selectivity than previously identified compounds. X-ray co-crystal structures indicate that these inhibitors bind in a conformation different from that of native substrates, enabling inhibition without acting as a substrate. Additionally, these new compounds effectively reduce CS levels in tumors in mice and, as such, have potential as cancer therapeutics in combination with ICB therapy.

article.title: Oncogenic modulation of MAPK signaling in leukemia via SPNS2-driven sphingolipid metabolism and membrane nanodomains remodeling
article.authors: Gaetano Sodaro; Khansa Saadallah; Swann Bredin; Michel Kahi; Frank Ling; Paul-Arthur Meslin; Hélène Pasquer; Christopher F. Bassil; Jonathan Paz Montoya; Jean Andrea Maillat; Julie Lesieur; Chloé Zédouard; Nario Tomishige; Nina Fenouille; Matthieu Duchmann; Raphaël Itzykson; Arnaud Jacquel; Patrick Auberger; Kris C. Wood; Toshihide Kobayashi; Camille Lobry; Giovanni D’Angelo; Lina Benajiba; Alexandre Puissant
article.abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78821-1 Altered lipid metabolism is linked to cancer progression. Here, authors show that loss of sphingosine-1-phosphate transporter SPNS2 accelerates leukemia growth by modulating sphingolipid metabolism and potentiating MAPK signaling.

article.title: The transcription factor BCL11A restores differentiation potential to aged oligodendrocyte progenitor cells
article.authors: writetotanay@gmail.com (Amar Sharma); writetotanay@gmail.com (András Lakatos); writetotanay@gmail.com (Chao Zhao); writetotanay@gmail.com (Nick Goldman); writetotanay@gmail.com (Robin JM Franklin); writetotanay@gmail.com (Roey Baror); writetotanay@gmail.com (Tanay Ghosh); writetotanay@gmail.com (Wing Hei Au)
article.abstract: In young animals, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) in the CNS efficiently differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs), whereas ageing reduces this capacity, impairing remyelination following demyelinating injury and adaptive myelination involved in learning. To identify factors that restore resilience in aged OPCs, we developed gSWITCH ( https://altoslabs.shinyapps.io/gSWITCH/ , https://github.com/Tanay-math/gSWITCH ), a computational pipeline that captures dynamic gene-expression patterns to identify ‘switch’ genes during lineage progression and ordered biological transitions, including time-series experiments. gSWITCH identified OPC-characteristic switch genes, which we compared between young and aged OPCs to determine whether their regulation is altered with ageing. This revealed several transcription factors with reduced expression in aged OPCs. Transcription-factor binding-site enrichment highlighted Bcl11a as a potential master-regulator of multiple switch genes. Bcl11a inhibition reduced OPC differentiation into OLs, whereas its overexpression in aged OPCs significantly enhanced OL differentiation without affecting proliferation. In aged mice subjected to demyelination injury in spinal cord white matter, Bcl11a overexpression increased OPC differentiation within lesions. We found that Bcl11a has undergone pervasive purifying selection throughout vertebrate evolution, preserving its amino acid sequence by eliminating deleterious mutations. Our study shows that reversing the age-related decline of this evolutionarily conserved factor in aged OPCs restores their impaired capacity for differentiation.

article.title: Intergenerational Communication and Engagement Between Older Adults and Younger Generations in Asia: A Systematic Review
article.authors: Soon Lean Keng; Low Kim Lian
article.abstract: Abstract Background: Population ageing has increased the importance of social relationships and engagement for older adults. Intergenerational communication and engagement may strengthen social connectedness and support healthy ageing. Objective: To systematically review and synthesise evidence on outcomes associated with intergenerational communication and engagement between older adults and younger generations in Asian settings. Methods: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. Seven electronic databases were searched: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Embase and ScienceDirect. Eligible English-language quantitative, qualitative or mixed-methods studies examined intergenerational communication or engagement involving older adults and younger generations in Asian settings and were published between January 2020 and June 2026. Eligible studies were narratively synthesised. Results: Nine studies conducted in China, Taiwan and Singapore were included. Three outcome domains emerged: psychological well-being, social connectedness and healthy ageing. Intergenerational engagement was associated with reduced depressive symptoms and loneliness, enhanced self-esteem and life satisfaction, stronger social relationships, greater social participation and improvements in selected health-related behaviours. Conclusions: Intergenerational communication and engagement may support psychological well-being, social connectedness and selected dimensions of healthy ageing among older adults in Asian settings. Culturally appropriate approaches may foster inclusive and age-friendly communities. Further longitudinal and well-controlled research is needed.

article.title: The rise in prevalence of autoantibodies neutralizing type I interferons reaches a plateau in centenarians.
article.authors: Nanna Mørk; Julie A Jensen; Paul Bastard; Lisbeth Aagaard Larsen; Bettina Bundgaard; Marianne Nygaard; Signe Bedsted Clemmensen; Chiaki Tao; Vibeke Sorensen Catts; Anne Puel; Guillaume Vogt; Ivan David Lozada-Martinez; Juan-Manuel Anaya; Yasumichi Arai; Sachdev Singh Perminder; Satoshi Okada; Jean-Laurent Casanova; Kaare Christensen; Aurélie Cobat; Trine H Mogensen
article.abstract: While autoantibodies (auto-Abs) neutralizing type I interferons (IFN-I) are relatively rare before the age of 65 ( 6% in individuals above 80 years in the general population. To assess the prevalence of IFN-I auto-Abs at the extreme end of human lifespan, we performed a multinational study of centenarians from four geographically and ethnically distinct cohorts collected in Denmark (n = 258), Colombia (n = 99), Australia (n = 281), and Japan (n = 300), comprising 938 individuals. Across cohorts, 51/938 centenarians (5.4%) harbored auto-Abs neutralizing IFN-I, ranging from 3.3% (Japan) to 9.1% (Colombia). We found that the prevalence of IFN-I auto-Abs levels off in centenarians compared with individuals ≥80 years from the general population, demonstrating that neutralizing IFN-I auto-Abs are not incompatible with longevity, despite conferring a risk of life-threatening viral infections. Yet, the plateau of their prevalence in centenarians suggests that they may not be beneficial for reaching exceptional longevity and may negatively impact mortality.

article.title: Stress-inducible WASF3 regulates brain metabolism and cognitive function.
article.authors: Abu M Syed; Jin Ma; Ping-Yuan Wang; Youlim Son; Rozhin Penjweini; Nikhil Mattu; Jay R Knutson; Sachiko Nakamori-Yamashita; Danielle A Springer; Ananya Ganguly; Chengyu Liu; Paul M Hwang
article.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
article.abstract: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein family member 3 (WASF3) disrupts mitochondrial respiration and is induced in association with endoplasmic reticulum stress in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Because cognitive impairment is a hallmark of ME/CFS, we investigated the role of WASF3 in brain metabolism and function using WASF3 transgenic and knockout mouse models. WASF3 disrupted respiratory complex IV and localized to mitochondria-associated membranes, known to modulate cellular processes important for neuronal activity. Overexpression of WASF3 in the hippocampus, a critical region for memory formation, induced a metabolic shift toward glycolysis and promoted a "hypometabolic" state. Increased WASF3 also caused a reduction in ATPIF1, previously shown to facilitate cognitive function, and impaired learning. Conversely, WASF3 deficiency increased ATPIF1 level, enhanced oxidative metabolism, and preserved cognitive function under stress. Together, these findings demonstrate that WASF3 suppresses oxidative metabolism in the brain and contributes to cognitive dysfunction, providing mechanistic insights into the "brain fog" reported in ME/CFS.

article.title: Vanin-pantethine metabolic axis shapes dendritic cell function and affects inflammatory disorder progression.
article.authors: Ai-Ping Cao; Jun-Cheng Li; Rui Wang; Yun-Ying Wang; Nan Wu; Yan-Hong Liu; Zhi Jin; Jia-Yu Liu; Yan-Yan Shen; Yue Guo; Qi Qi; Yao Wang; Rui-Bo Wang; Bo-Yang Xie; Chun-Yan Yan; Qiu-Ying Han; Shao-Yi Huang; Sheng-Ming Wu; Na Wang; Xin Pan; Cheng-Xin Li; Tao Zhou; Ai-Ling Li; Qing Xia; Wei-Na Zhang
article.abstract: Aberrant activation of dendritic cells (DCs) is intricately associated with inflammatory diseases, rendering DCs an appealing therapeutic target. Metabolites are emerging as crucial regulators of DCs, yet therapeutic strategies targeting DC metabolism for inflammatory diseases remain underexplored. Our study identifies the Vanin-pantethine-cholesterol axis as a key metabolic pathway that governs DC activation-a classical APC function. We found that Vanin is upregulated in activated DCs from autoimmune patients and mice; DC-specific Vanin deficiency significantly alleviates psoriasiform inflammation in mice. Mechanistically, Vanin hydrolyzes pantethine, leading to cholesterol and lipid raft accumulation on the cell membrane and promoting DC hyperactivation. Pantethine supplementation or pharmacologically induced Vanin inhibition reduces cholesterol overload, impedes DC activation, and mitigates psoriasiform inflammation. Notably, pantethine or RR6 treatment impairs activation of patient-derived DCs, and our investigator-initiated trial shows that pantethine combination therapy relieves clinical symptoms in psoriasis patients. Collectively, these findings establish the Vanin-pantethine-cholesterol axis as a key modulator of APC function, offering a promising metabolic approach for inflammatory diseases.

article.title: Increasing autophagy with fasting and diet: separating fact from fiction.
article.authors: Sanjna Singh; Timothy J Sargeant
article.abstract: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system; it removes unwanted or dysfunctional cellular material, thereby preventing damage. Importantly, it is a key pro-survival pathway during periods of stress, for instance, during nutrient scarcity. As it can support nutrition during starvation, it is not surprising that autophagy is controlled by nutrient availability. As a result, diet-based strategies to modify autophagy have attracted considerable scientific and public interest, although what is presented to the public is often not supported by a solid scientific foundation. Evidence from animal models is compelling: several of these interventions robustly activate autophagy and are linked to improved lifespan and healthspan. Data from humans, however, are much more limited. Many human studies rely on measurement of steady-state levels of autophagy genes or proteins, metrics that do not independently establish pathway activity. Far fewer have measured autophagic 'flux', the more rigorous readout of turnover, and where they have, findings are often negative or inconclusive. Here, we review the human research on popular nutritional interventions purported to change autophagy-including prolonged fasting, intermittent fasting, calorie restriction, and altered macronutrient intake-and contrast these findings with the preclinical evidence that has shaped public expectations. We highlight key gaps in the literature, particularly the scarcity of flux-based measurements and the reliance on blood as a proxy for autophagy in other, less accessible tissues. Refining how we monitor autophagy in humans should be a key priority for the field and is ultimately needed to establish whether and how diet modulates human autophagy.

article.title: Recent advances in understanding the regulatory mechanisms of P4-ATPase lipid flippases.
article.authors: Pauline Funke; Mathilde Roth; Thibaud Dieudonné; Guillaume Lenoir
article.abstract: P4-ATPases establish and maintain transbilayer lipid asymmetry in eukaryotic membranes by transporting phospholipids from the exoplasmic to the cytosolic membrane leaflet at the expense of ATP hydrolysis. In recent years, biochemical analysis together with an increasing number of cryo-electron microscopy structures has substantially increased our understanding of the lipid transport cycle and substrate recognition by P4-ATPases. However, the underlying molecular mechanism governing P4-ATPase activation and regulation remains less well understood. The present review aims to summarize current insights into the molecular mechanisms controlling P4-ATPase activation and regulation. We discuss autoinhibition by N- and C-terminal extensions, activation by regulatory lipids, particularly phosphoinositides, regulation by interacting proteins including small GTPases and guanine nucleotide exchange factors, and post-translational modifications, especially phosphorylation. Together, these studies reveal that P4-ATPase activity is controlled by a complex and multilayered regulatory network that enables precise control of lipid transport. Future studies combining structural, biochemical, and cellular approaches will be essential to elucidate how these mechanisms cooperate to maintain membrane lipid homeostasis and support diverse cellular functions.

article.title: Diverse RNA Editing Systems Across Heterolobosea (Discoba).
article.authors: Seda Mirzoyan; Pia Corre; Eliska Zadrobilkova; Tomas Panek
article.abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

article.title: A ubiquitin network safeguards cell identity by continuously degrading a stem cell-related translational machinery.
article.authors: Salwa Danial; Raya Ghanim; Muhammad Makhzumy; Avital Oknin Vaisman; Eliya Bitman-Lotan; Fabian Glaser; Jelly Soffers; Jesslyn C Henriksen; Avital Sarusi-Portuguez; Olivia S Rissland; Ryan D Mohan; Ayala Shiber; Amir Orian
article.abstract: How cell identity is maintained is a fundamental question, and loss of cell identity is a hallmark of aging associated with multiple age-related diseases. In the adult Drosophila midgut, we identified a posttranscriptional regulatory layer that supervises enterocyte (EC) identity and fails upon aging. Combining single-cell RNA-seq with lineage tracing in aging ECs and classical genetics, we found that aging ECs express genes that unlock the differentiated state. Upon aging, the protein Rogue (CG13928), a translational repressor, along with its partner, Orb2, orchestrates reactivation of a stem cell-related translational repression machinery involving P-body-associated RNA-binding proteins canceling the differentiated state. In young ECs, this machinery is continuously suppressed by the deubiquitinase nonstop (dUSP22) and the ubiquitin E2 dUbcH8/Kdo and E3 CTLH complex, mediating the degradation of the stem cell-related RNA binding proteins safeguarding EC identity. Upon aging, levels of dUSP22 decline and Rogue is ectopically expressed. RNA immunoprecipitation followed by nanopore-based direct RNA sequencing identified that Rogue binds to the RNA transcripts of dUbcH8/Kdo and eEF2, shortening their poly(A) tail and suppressing Kdo protein, resulting in accelerated proteasomal clearance of the CTLH complex. Subsequently, the stem cell-related P-bodies are reactivated, leading to decline in EC gene signatures and unlocking EC identity.

article.title: Mechanistic study on the promotion of osteogenic differentiation in osteoporotic rats by moxibustion via regulation of BMSCs-derived exosomal miR-27a-3p-mediated mitophagy.
article.authors: Xing Li; Xiao Li; Adi Wirawan Tjahjono; Xiaoli Chen; Lu Cui; Paradi Sangvatanakul; Xiaojuan Hong; Xiang Li
article.abstract: AIMS: To investigate the effects of moxibustion (MOX) on bone loss and osteogenic differentiation in ovariectomized (OVX) rats and determine whether these effects are mediated by mitophagy through bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs)-derived exosomal miR-27a-3p. METHODS: The study was conducted in three stages. In stage 1, sham-operated (SO), OVX, and OVX + MOX rats were evaluated by micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) to assess bone mass and by Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining to evaluate osteogenic differentiation. Autophagy-related markers were also examined, and mitochondrial-lysosomal colocalization was assessed by immunofluorescence. In stage 2, the mitophagy inhibitor Mdivi-1 was administered to OVX + MOX rats to determine the contribution of mitophagy to the effects of MOX. Sequencing analysis and TargetScan prediction identified a potential regulatory relationship between miR-27a-3p and the mitophagy-related gene PINK1, which was subsequently validated using a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In stage 3, miR-27a-3p agomir and antagomir were used to investigate the involvement of the miR-27a-3p-mitophagy axis. RESULTS: MOX increased bone mineral density, improved bone microarchitecture, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation in OVX rats, accompanied by increased mitophagy. Mdivi-1 attenuated these beneficial effects, exacerbating bone loss and reducing osteogenic gene expression, mineralized nodule formation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitophagy. The dual-luciferase reporter assay confirmed that PINK1 is a direct target of miR-27a-3p. Inhibition of miR-27a-3p with an antagomir impaired bone microarchitecture, mitophagy, and osteogenesis. Conversely, MOX produced effects comparable to those of the miR-27a-3p agomir, with both interventions promoting osteogenic differentiation through the miR-27a-3p-mitophagy axis. CONCLUSIONS: MOX attenuates bone loss in OVX-induced osteoporosis (OP) by promoting osteogenic differentiation. These effects may be mediated, at least in part, by activation of mitophagy through the BMSCs-associated miR-27a-3p/PINK1 axis, providing a potential mechanistic basis for the therapeutic effects of MOX in OP.

article.title: SphK1/S1P signaling network: From molecular mechanism to therapeutic targeting.
article.authors: Duxiao Yang; Zhen Wang
article.abstract: Sphingosine kinase 1 (SphK1) is a key rate-limiting enzyme in the sphingolipid metabolic network. It generates sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) by catalyzing the phosphorylation of Sphingosine (Sph). It plays a key regulatory role in various physiological and pathological processes such as cell proliferation, survival, migration, inflammatory response and immune regulation. SphK1 closely connects intracellular lipid metabolism with extracellular GPCR signaling network, forming a complex "inside-out" signal transduction system. In this review, we focus on the current understanding of SphK1, including its structure characteristics, activation mechanism and signal transduction pathway. We also review the roles of SphK1 pathway in tumor, inflammation and immunity, cardiovascular, nervous system, digestive system, respiratory system and metabolic disease. Establishing a correlation between SphK1 or the SphK1/S1P signal axis and targeted drugs such as inhibitors, agonists, even some natural Chinese medicines, provides important theoretical support for understanding the potential of SphK1 as a therapeutic target. Finally, we propose future research directions based on current advances and shortcomings.

article.title: CDK5/Drp1-mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction Drives 1-Bromopropane-induced Hippocampal Neurotoxicity in Mice.
article.authors: Mingxue Song; Liwen Zhang; Caipei Liu; Ruifang Liu; Fuyong Song; Xiulan Zhao
article.abstract: Occupational exposure to 1-bromopropane (1-BP) has been linked to impairments in learning and memory; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely defined. Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), a critical regulator of neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, is aberrantly activated in multiple neurodegenerative conditions and toxin-induced neuronal injury. Here, we investigated whether CDK5 contributes to 1-BP-induced hippocampal neurotoxicity by promoting mitochondrial dysfunction. Using mouse and N2a cell models, we showed that 1-BP exposure triggered calpain-mediated proteolysis, increased p25 generation, and enhanced CDK5 activation in hippocampal neurons and N2a cells. CDK5 activation was accompanied by elevated Drp1 expression and phosphorylation, indicative of excessive mitochondrial fission and fragmentation. These mitochondrial abnormalities were associated with neuronal death, as evidenced by increased TUNEL-positive cells and upregulation of the necroptosis-related proteins RIPK1 and MLKL. Pharmacological inhibition of CDK5 with roscovitine markedly suppressed 1-BP-induced mitochondrial fission and neuronal necroptosisin N2a cells. Consistently, heterozygous Cdk5 haploinsufficiency mitigated mitochondrial structural and functional damage, reduced hippocampal neuronal loss, and improved learning and memory deficits in 1-BP-exposed mice. Together, these findings identify the CDK5/Drp1 axis as a critical mediator of 1-BP-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and hippocampal neuronal injury, providing mechanistic insight into the neurotoxicity of 1-BP.

article.title: A structure-based virtual screening-driven discovery pharmaceutics platform for cancer therapeutics development: FDA 505(b)(2) repurposing of netupitant as a BMX-targeted nanomedicine using quality-by-design lipid nanoparticles and model-informed PBPK translation.
article.authors: Manasa Singirikonda; Tarang Patel; Prashanth Parupathi; Akshaya Nagarajan; Jainam Shaileshkumar Patel; Lakshmisirisha Devarakonda; Avinash Kumar; Kenza E Benzeroual; Rutesh H Dave; Mouhannad Jumaa; Suliman Al-Fayoumi; Sami Nazzal; Ahmed Abu Fayyad
article.abstract: Bone marrow tyrosine kinase on chromosome X (BMX) is an emerging therapeutic target implicated in prostate cancer progression, metastatic disease, and resistance to current therapies; however, no selective BMX-targeted therapy has advanced to clinical development. Building upon our previously established AI-driven BMX discovery platform, this study presents an integrated Discovery Pharmaceutics strategy combining artificial intelligence-assisted drug repurposing, Quality-by-Design (QbD)-guided lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, experimental validation, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling to accelerate clinical translation through the FDA 505(b)(2) regulatory pathway. An structure-based virtual screening workflow comprising 2,115 FDA-approved small molecules identified netupitant as one of the highest-ranked candidates against the BMX catalytic domain, exhibiting a predicted binding affinity of -10.9 kcal/mol together with favorable selectivity over closely related Tec-family kinases. Netupitant demonstrated concentration-dependent inhibition of prostate cancer cell growth with IC50 values of 15.97 μM in DU145 cells and 7.1 μM in PC3 cells. A Box-Behnken Design optimized Netupitant-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Netupitant-LNPs) with a particle size of 133.9 ± 3.2 nm, polydispersity index of 0.213 ± 0.005, zeta potential of + 30 ± 1.3 mV, and encapsulation efficiency of 97.3 ± 0.7%. Cryogenic transmission electron microscopy confirmed uniformly dispersed spherical nanoparticles with an average diameter of 130 ± 6 nm, consistent with dynamic light scattering measurements. The nanoformulation substantially enhanced therapeutic efficacy, reducing IC50 values to 1.1 μM in DU145 cells and 0.5 μM in PC3 cells, representing approximately 15-fold and 14-fold improvements, respectively, over free netupitant. To facilitate clinical translation, experimentally determined formulation characteristics were incorporated into a mechanistic Simcyp® Version 25.2 middle-out physiologically based pharmacokinetic model. The exploratory PBPK model compared alternative intravenous dosing scenarios and identified 100 mg once weekly as a candidate regimen for further evaluation; these simulations do not establish a clinical dosing recommendation. Collectively, this work demonstrates that integrating AI-enabled drug repurposing, Discovery Pharmaceutics, nanomedicine engineering, and model-informed drug development provides an effective strategy for accelerating oncology drug development. Netupitant-LNPs emerge as a repurposed nanomedicine candidate with predicted BMX binding while establishing a broadly applicable translational framework for FDA-approved drug repurposing through the 505(b)(2) pathway.

article.title: M6A-modified lncRNA RMRP facilitates mitophagy and promotes ox-LDL-induced endothelial cell injury by interacting with PTBP1 and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway.
article.authors: Ying Fu; Zhu Zhang; Yanqin Yu; Yuanmin Chai; Jinqi Hao; Qinghong Qiao
article.venue: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Gene regulatory mechanisms
article.abstract: BACKGROUND: Endothelial cell dysfunction has been identified as a major risk factor for atherosclerosis. The long non-coding RNA (LncRNA) RNA component of mitochondrial RNA processing endoribonuclease (RMRP) has been detected in mitochondria and is closely associated with inflammation and autophagy. However, the role of the lncRNA RMRP in endothelial cell injury and its potential molecular mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: Mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs) were treated with oxidised low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL). Changes in cell viability, proinflammatory cytokine levels, mitophagy, and mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs were assessed to investigate the effects of lncRNA RMRP and protein kinase B (AKT3) on endothelial injury. Knockdown and overexpression experiments were performed to determine the effects of lncRNA RMRP, polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (PTBP1), and AKT3 on MAECs stimulated with ox-LDL. RESULTS: Ox-LDL markedly reduced cell viability, increased proinflammatory factor levels, induced mitophagy, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs. Knockdown of lncRNA RMRP attenuated ox-LDL-induced inflammatory responses and mitophagy in MAECs. Knockdown of Methyltransferase-like 14 (METTL14) suppressed the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification in ox-LDL-treated MAECs. LncRNA RMRP enhanced AKT3 mRNA stability by interacting with PTBP1. LncRNA RMRP promoted ox-LDL-induced mitophagy by targeting AKT3 and stimulating the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT pathway in MAECs. CONCLUSION: METTL14 regulates the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification. Overexpressed lncRNA RMRP targets AKT3 by recruiting PTBP1, thus activating the PI3K/AKT pathway to mediate mitophagy and promote the progression of atherosclerosis.

article.title: TDP-43 dysfunction destabilizes glial homeostatic identity in ALS/FTD.
article.authors: Anna Dale; Rita Sattler
article.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) pathology is a defining feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Although TDP-43 dysfunction has traditionally been studied through a neuron-centric framework, increasing evidence demonstrates that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes are also directly affected and actively contribute to disease progression. In this review, we examine how TDP-43 dysfunction disrupts lineage-specific glial homeostatic programs and promotes distinct pathological state transitions across major glial populations. In astrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction impairs neurotransmitter regulation, metabolic and neuronal support, RNA homeostasis, and secretory signaling while promoting inflammatory and antiviral-like states. In microglia, altered TDP-43 disrupts inflammatory regulation, phagocytosis, lysosomal function, lipid metabolism, and stage-dependent protective responses. In oligodendrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction compromises RNA processing, lineage maintenance, lipid metabolism, myelin integrity, and long-term axonal support. Together, these findings suggest that glial TDP-43 dysfunction cannot be reduced to a single generalized form of reactivity but instead reflects the breakdown of distinct cell type-specific identities required to maintain central nervous system homeostasis. A cross-glial framework integrating cell-autonomous dysfunction, non-cell-autonomous signaling, disease stage, and genetic context may therefore provide a more complete understanding of TDP-43 proteinopathy and its contribution to neurodegeneration across the ALS-FTD spectrum.

article.title: Structure-property relationships in series of hydroxypropyl-functionalized imidazolium surfactants: linking self-assembly, lipid bilayer interactions, and antimicrobial activity.
article.authors: Darya A Kuznetsova; Denis M Kuznetsov; Veronica S Kolbasina; Anna P Lubina; Alexandra D Voloshina; Lucia Ya Zakharova
article.venue: Biochimica et biophysica acta. General subjects
article.abstract: Hydroxyalkyl-functionalized cationic surfactants are promising membrane-active compounds with potential antimicrobial applications. In this work, a homologous series of hydroxypropyl-substituted imidazolium surfactants (HPIm-n, n = 12, 14, 16, and 18) was investigated with respect to self-assembly, solubilization, membrane interactions, and antimicrobial activity. The surfactants exhibited pronounced amphiphilic properties and formed positively charged aggregates in aqueous solution, with the critical micelle concentration decreasing from 2.6 to 0.17 mM with increasing alkyl chain length. Self-assembly was strongly affected by the ionic environment, with lower aggregation thresholds and altered aggregate properties observed in phosphate-buffered saline compared with deionized water. The surfactants showed chain-length-dependent solubilization of hydrophobic compounds, while their interactions with DPPC and DPPC/DPPG (70,30 mol%) liposomes revealed pronounced effects on lipid phase behavior and membrane surface charge. Calcein leakage from DPPC/DPPG liposomes demonstrated a structure-dependent membrane-permeabilizing effect, with HPIm-14 showing the highest activity. Antimicrobial activity also depended strongly on alkyl chain length, with HPIm-14 and HPIm-16 showing the highest activity and MIC values as low as 0.9 μM against Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Overall, the results demonstrate that alkyl chain length and ionic environment are important determinants of the self-assembly, solubilization, membrane interactions, and antimicrobial activity of hydroxypropyl-substituted imidazolium surfactants.

article.title: Sodium propionate alleviates ammonia toxicity by enhancing intestinal ammonia capture by α-ketoglutarate in yellow catfish (Pelteobagrus fulvidraco) under chronic ammonia stress.
article.authors: Shidong Wang; Xue Li; Ming Li; Muzi Zhang; Ying Liu
article.venue: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Toxicology & pharmacology : CBP
article.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of dietary sodium propionate (SP) supplementation on growth performance, physiological health, intestinal metabolism, and microbiota composition in yellow catfish under chronic ammonia stress (CAS), and elucidated the mechanisms underlying ammonia detoxification. A total of 360 juvenile yellow catfish were randomly assigned to four groups: fish fed 0% SP under 0 mg/L total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) (CON), fish fed 0% SP under 50 mg/L TAN (AM), fish fed 1% SP under 0 mg/L TAN (SP), fish fed 1% SP under 50 mg/L TAN (SPAM). Compared with the AM group, the SPAM group showed increases in weight gain rate and specific growth rate of 74.07% and 39.17%, respectively, and a decrease in feed conversion ratio of 33.12% (P < 0.05). These results indicate that SP alleviates CAS induced growth inhibition. Compared with the AM group, the SPAM group exhibited increases in serum superoxide dismutase and catalase activities of 31.30% and 30.13%, respectively, and decreases hydrogen peroxide, ammonia, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, triglyceride, total cholesterol, and glucose levels of 51.41%, 27.89%, 82.72%, 41.81%, 22.27%, 51.91%, and 28.23%, respectively (P < 0.05). These results indicate that SP alleviates CAS induced elevations in serum ammonia, impairment of antioxidant defenses, and disturbances in physiological indices. Furthermore, SP upregulated acyl-CoA synthetase short-chain family member 2 (ACSS2), propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunit alpha (PCCA), isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1), and glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (GLUD1) (P < 0.05) protein expression level. Meanwhile, intestinal metabolomic analysis revealed that SP increased propionyl-CoA, succinate, α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), and glutamate levels. These data indicated that propionate is converted to α-KG through the ACSS2/PCCA/IDH1 pathway. Subsequently, GLUD1-mediated reductive amination of α-KG captures ammonia to generate non-toxic glutamate. Microbiota analysis showed that SP increased the abundance of beneficial Cetobacterium. Collectively, dietary SP alleviates ammonia toxicity through synergistic regulation of host ACSS2/PCCA/IDH1/GLUD1-mediated ammonia assimilation and Cetobacterium enrichment.

article.title: Mitochondrial Transplantation as a Therapeutic Strategy: From Energy Replacement to Metabolic and Immune Reprogramming.
article.authors: Chuli Zhu; Meng Xu; Yanan Ji; Jie Wang; Xinlei Yao; Hualin Sun
article.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction drives diseases, including ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and inflammation. Conventional mitochondria-targeted strategies offer only partial rescue and are insufficient for severe, irreversible damage. Mitochondrial transplantation (MT)-the delivery of exogenously isolated functional mitochondria to injured cells-has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy that directly restores mitochondrial bioenergetic function and may subsequently modify the tissue microenvironment. This Review examines the entire MT pipeline, from mitochondrial source selection, isolation and preservation, to in vivo delivery strategies. We critically examine the multiple mechanisms underlying MT's therapeutic efficacy, including cellular uptake and intracellular integration, energy restoration and metabolic reprogramming, redox rebalancing, remodeling of mitochondrial quality control (fusion/fission, mitophagy, biogenesis), and immunomodulation. We summarize preclinical and clinical applications across multiple organ systems-heart, nervous system, liver, kidney, lung, skeletal muscle, retina-as well as in oncology and aging. We analyze five major translational bottlenecks: the lack of standardized manufacturing protocols, undefined dose-response relationships, immunogenicity and long-term safety uncertainties, the decisive impact of mitochondrial heterogeneity, and regulatory ambiguity. We outline future directions-mechanistic deepening, engineered target delivery, individualized mitochondrial medicine, combinatorial regimens, and a phased clinical roadmap. MT is not merely energy supplementation; it may reshape cellular metabolism, quality control networks, and immune microenvironments, representing a shift from pharmacological modulation of mitochondrial function toward organelle replacement strategies. Despite challenges, these advances may facilitate individualized mitochondrial therapies as a proposed future direction.

article.title: Role and mechanism of action of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in nonylphenol-induced podocyte apoptosis and glomerulonephritis.
article.authors: Chengxing Wang; Jie Xu; Yuzhu Xu; Ya Luo; Jie Yu
article.abstract: Podocyte injury is an early and critical event in the development of glomerulonephritis (GN). Nonylphenol (NP) can accumulate in the kidney and induce nephrotoxicity. However, the mechanism by which NP promotes GN progression by inducing podocyte apoptosis remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether NP exposure activated PTEN-induced kinase 1/Parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (PINK1/Parkin)-mediated mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial homeostasis imbalance in podocytes and promoting apoptosis, thereby inducing pathological changes associated with GN in mice. Cell experiments were performed in Mouse Podocyte Clone-5 (MPC-5) cells by activating or inhibiting Parkin. In vivo, 72 male wild-type and Parkin-/- C57BL/6 mice were treated with different doses of NP by gavage for 90 days to investigate the role of Parkin in NP-induced renal injury. The results showed that NP exposure activated the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy pathway in MPC-5 cells and was accompanied by increased apoptosis and inflammatory responses. Parkin inhibition impaired mitophagy and exacerbated NP-induced cellular injury, whereas Parkin activation enhanced mitophagy and attenuated inflammation and apoptosis, indicating a cytoprotective role of Parkin. Consistently, NP exposure for 90 days induced renal dysfunction, podocyte injury, mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, inflammation, apoptosis, and activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in mice. These alterations were further aggravated in Parkin-/- mice, which exhibited impaired autophagy and more severe mitochondrial and renal injury. Collectively, Parkin-mediated mitophagy plays a key protective role in maintaining podocyte homeostasis and alleviating glomerular structural and functional damage.

article.title: Lysosomal biophysics in CLN3 disease: Connecting membrane transport, molecular homeostasis, and tissue dysfunction.
article.authors: Najla Khaled Al Abdulsalam; Rabab S Hamad; Elsayed A Elmorsy; Sameh Saber
article.venue: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
article.abstract: CLN3 disease (CLN3 Batten disease) is a lysosomal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early retinal degeneration and progressive neurological dysfunction, yet the mechanisms connecting CLN3-dependent membrane physiology to selective cellular and tissue vulnerability remain unresolved. This review integrates current evidence across four experimentally separable scales: membrane biophysics, molecular and organellar homeostasis, cell-specific function, and tissue pathology. Direct electrophysiological studies support a luminal pH-sensitive CLN3-dependent lysosomal chloride conductance associated, in tested systems, with changes in luminal chloride, pH, cathepsin activity, and protein degradation. Independently, CLN3 deficiency disrupts glycerophosphodiester clearance, phospholipid and cholesterol handling, cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor trafficking, hydrolase delivery, and autophagic lysosomal reformation. These organellar abnormalities coexist with distinct phenotypes in retinal pigment epithelium, neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and brain endothelial cells, together with retinal, neural-circuit, and myelin abnormalities at the tissue level. Current evidence does not establish a universal chloride-first or storage-first cascade; instead, it supports interacting CLN3-dependent modules whose causal ordering may vary by cell type, model, and disease stage. We therefore propose a multiscale mechanistic framework that links measurable lysosomal physical variables to molecular homeostasis, cell-specific function, and tissue vulnerability while preserving the distinction between direct evidence and mechanistic inference. This framework defines testable priorities for causal ordering, rescue experiments, and mechanism-matched target engagement in CLN3 disease.

article.title: Hemocytes as nutrient-sensing regulators of immune function, lifespan, and intergenerational fitness in Drosophila melanogaster.
article.authors: Seyhmus Bayar; Elvira Mass
article.abstract: Hemocytes are the primary cellular components of the innate immune system in Drosophila melanogaster and share functional and molecular characteristics with vertebrate myeloid cells. They arise in two developmental waves, an embryonic and a larval wave, and persist through metamorphosis into the adult fly, where they carry out phagocytosis, melanisation, encapsulation, and cytokine signalling. Because hemocytes are in contact with the hemolymph throughout life, they register the nutritional state of the organism through conserved nutrient-sensing pathways, including insulin-like signalling, the target of rapamycin, adipokinetic hormone, and glucose transport. Signalling through these pathways can influence hemocyte metabolism and function, and hemocyte-derived signals can in turn affect systemic metabolism, fitness, and lifespan. Growing evidence indicates that these effects are not confined to the exposed individual, since parental and in particular maternal diet can alter hemocyte number, composition, and immune capability in the progeny. In this review, we discuss the ontogeny of Drosophila hemocytes across the life cycle, their contribution to immune ageing and lifespan, and the nutrient-sensing pathways through which they translate dietary input into altered immune function. We further examine the intergenerational consequences of maternal diet for hemocyte programming, drawing parallels with the developmental programming of tissue-resident macrophages in mammals. Understanding hemocytes as nutrient-sensing regulators may clarify how diet shapes immune function and survival across generations.

article.title: Aging reshapes the response to subchronic LPS: cognitive and neuroinflammatory resilience with selective amyloid vulnerability and reduced responsiveness to L-Theanine and aerobic exercise.
article.authors: Jana Tchekalarova; Georgi Hadzhipetrov; Petja Ivanova; Desislava Krushovlieva; Katerina Georgieva
article.abstract: Aging alters the brain's inflammatory profile, which may influence vulnerability to neuroinflammatory insults and the effectiveness of neuroprotective interventions. This study investigated whether prophylactic administration of L-theanine (LT) and aerobic exercise could attenuate behavioral and molecular changes induced by subchronic systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) exposure in aged rats. Three- and eighteen-month-old male Wistar rats received LT, exercise, or both prior to repeated LPS administration. Behavioral assessments included working, recognition, and spatial short-term memory, followed by hippocampal analyses of inflammatory cytokines, the pCREB/CREB ratio, and Aβ₁-₄₂ expression. Both aging and LPS administration in 3-month-old rats impaired working memory, spatial short-term memory, and motor activity compared to young adult controls. Unlike young adult animals, subchronic LPS exposure did not impair cognitive performance in aged rats. LPS exposure resulted in reduced body weight and increased Aβ₁-₄₂ levels, while IL-1β, TNF-α, and the pCREB/CREB ratio remained unchanged in aged rats. Prophylactic LT and/or aerobic exercise produced modest behavioral improvements, enhancing working memory in the Y-maze, but did not significantly alter hippocampal inflammatory cytokines, the pCREB/CREB ratio, or Aβ₁-₄₂ expression in old rats. In conclusion, aged rats exhibited relative resistance to LPS-induced cognitive and inflammatory effects but remained susceptible to amyloid-related changes.

article.title: The deubiquitinase OTUD1 aggravated dopaminergic neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease model by promoting the degradation of Parkin.
article.authors: Mengting Wu; Tengfei Liu; Runzhe Zong; Lu Yu; Qiuran Ji; Ru Sun; Lin Chen; Huiqing Liu
article.abstract: Parkin plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), which reverse Parkin ubiquitination, are critical for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. Although ovarian tumor protease deubiquitinase 1 (OTUD1) participates in various biological processes, its specific functions in PD and its regulation of Parkin remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that OTUD1 expression was significantly elevated in the nigrostriatal region of PD patients and MPTP-induced PD mice. Genetic ablation of OTUD1 markedly improved motor deficits and attenuated dopaminergic neuronal loss in PD models. Mechanistically, OTUD1 worsened mitochondrial dysfunction in PD models by negatively regulating Parkin protein levels. OTUD1 interacted with Parkin and selectively removed K27- and K33-linked polyubiquitin chains through its DUB activity, leading to Parkin degradation via the autophagic-lysosomal pathway. Our findings identify OTUD1 as a negative regulator of Parkin and reveal a mechanism linking deubiquitination to mitochondrial dysfunction in PD, which offers a novel potential therapeutic target for PD.

article.title: Mitochondrial transfer in cancer-immune crosstalk.
article.authors: Yuhan Chen; Zhangui Tang; Jingyi Cheng
article.venue: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
article.abstract: Mitochondrial transfer has emerged as a pivotal mechanism of intercellular metabolic reprogramming within the tumor microenvironment (TME), fundamentally reshaping cancer-immune crosstalk. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the regulatory triggers, molecular routes, and functional consequences of mitochondrial transfer in the tumor immune microenvironment. Mitochondrial exchange between tumor and immune cells occurs bidirectionally via tunneling nanotubes, extracellular vesicles, and other pathways, and is dynamically regulated by reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic stress. We delineate how this transfer exerts dual effects on antitumor immunity: tumor cells hijack functional mitochondria from T cells, macrophages, and stromal cells to fuel their proliferation and therapy resistance, while simultaneously delivering mutant mitochondria to immune cells to drive exhaustion and immune evasion. Conversely, artificial mitochondrial transfer to immune cells-including repolarization of tumor-associated macrophages via M1-derived mitochondria and metabolic augmentation of T cells and natural killer cells-demonstrates significant potential to reinvigorate antitumor immunity and overcome resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. We further discuss emerging strategies to block pro-tumoral mitochondrial hijacking through cytoskeletal inhibitors and extracellular vesicle modulators. Critical challenges for clinical translation-including precision delivery, sustained functional integration, mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy risks, and interactions with conventional therapies-are also addressed. By integrating mechanistic insights with therapeutic innovation, this review positions mitochondrial transfer as both a targetable driver of immunosuppression and a platform for next-generation cancer immunotherapies.

article.title: Convergent Node, Divergent Failure: GPX4-SLC7A11-GSH Ferroptosis as a Unifying, Tissue-Decoded Axis of Diabetic Complications.
article.authors: Mutaz Jamal Al-Khreisat; Sarah Qutayba Badraldin; Jasur Rizaev; Mamura Kucharova; Djamila Polatova; Mrtda Adnan Mhysn; Navin Kumar Tailor
article.venue: The Journal of steroid biochemistry and molecular biology
article.abstract: Diabetic complications of the kidney, heart, retina, bone, β-cells, nervous system, vasculature, and reproductive organs have been studied as separate diseases. Iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation may be a unifying upstream vulnerability rather than the dominant death morphology; we organized the evidence into five levels. Metabolic ignition (L1) loads the substrate via glucolipotoxic polyunsaturated-fatty-acid/ACSL4 priming and ferritinophagic iron release. These pressures act on the central defense network (L2): glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), SLC7A11/xCT, and glutathione (GSH). Gain-of-function restoration attenuates diabetic injury, and loss-of-function evidence is correlative. We do not call this GPX4-dependent network rate-limiting; graded manipulation of endogenous GPX4 has not been performed in diabetic tissues. Glutathione-independent arms act in parallel but differ in status, GCH1-BH4 appears depleted, FSP1 uncharacterized, and DHODH unestablished and contested. Diabetes disables this node through transcriptional, post-translational, epigenetic, non-coding-RNA, and organelle-specific routes (L3) rather than one lesion. Each tissue decodes the same failure into a distinct organ program (L4) set by its architecture and functional demands, and shared regulators may act oppositely across compartments. Extracellular-vesicle and gut-organ axes couple these programs (L5a), but the insulin-resistance relationship is directionally unresolved: AMPK-NRF2-GPX4 evidence is limited and pharmacological, and glutathione peroxidase loss can itself improve insulin sensitivity. Translation (L5b) returns the same target: reduced GPX4 and SLC7A11 with elevated ACSL4 recurs across complications and is associated with severity. Evidence is predominantly preclinical, and human data are almost entirely observational. The framework is hypothesis-generating rather than clinically actionable, and the null-to-unfavorable record of global antioxidant and NRF2-directed trials indicates that interventions must be cell- and context-resolved.

article.title: Platycodin D Disrupts Human Sperm Function via the MAPK/p53 Pathway.
article.authors: Qing Hong; Yuting Jiang; Fangfang Liao; Qiong Liu
article.abstract: Platycodin D (PD), a natural triterpenoid saponin from Platycodon grandiflorum, exhibits cytotoxic and spermatotoxic properties. However, the specific mechanisms underlying its impairment of human sperm function are not fully understood. This study was designed to focus on the effects of PD on human sperm and the mechanisms. Human spermatozoa were exposed to PD (1-100 μM). PD treatment dose-dependently reduced sperm viability, motility, penetration capacity, capacitation, and acrosome reaction. Mechanistically, PD induced a significant, dose-dependent accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and concurrently disrupted the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Network pharmacology analysis predicted the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway as a key mediator of the effects of PD on sperm. Experimental validation via Western blotting confirmed that PD significantly upregulated phosphorylated MAPK3 (p-MAPK3) and phosphorylated p53 (p-p53), whereas total MAPK3 was also moderately increased, to a lesser extent than p-MAPK3, and total p53 levels remained unchanged. Furthermore, PD induced the upregulation of caspase-3, an indicator of apoptosis-like pathway activation. These findings suggest that PD-induced sperm dysfunction is associated with ROS accumulation, mitochondrial depolarization, and activation of the MAPK/p53 signaling axis. Further intervention studies are warranted to establish causal relationships.

article.title: Primary cilia mediate specific neuron-glia attachments in C. elegans through the secreted protein BUG-1.
article.authors: Leland R Wexler; Brian Griffin; Priya Dutta; Piali Sengupta; Irina Kolotuev; Niels Ringstad; Maxwell G Heiman
article.abstract: Primary cilia are signaling hubs that influence nearly every aspect of cell physiology. Neuronal primary cilia were recently found to form extensive attachments to glia in the mammalian brain, but it is not known how these attachments form or what functions they serve. Defects in cilia cause profound neurological disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the specialized functions of neuronal cilia. Here, we use a genetic screen in Caenorhabditis elegans to determine how a stereotyped cilia-glia attachment forms and how the attachment affects ciliary calcium signaling. We find that two sensory neurons (URX and BAG) use their cilia to attach to a specific glial partner (ILsoL/R). This attachment requires BUG-1, a large secreted protein that localizes precisely to the cilia-glia attachment site. In the absence of BUG-1, neuronal cilia are present but always fail to attach to the glial cell. As a result, the URX cilia do not undergo activity-dependent remodeling seen in wild-type neurons and the BAG cilia exhibit reduced sensory stimulus-evoked calcium entry and defects in calcium clearance. Our work shows that cilia can select specific glial partners for attachment, identifies a novel protein that mediates these attachments, and demonstrates the functional consequences of loss of cilia-glia attachment on neuronal signaling. We propose that neuronal primary cilia act not only as antennae to receive long-range signals but also as points of close-range cell-cell contact, through which glia could modulate neuronal signaling.

article.title: Macrophage lipid signaling drives glioblastoma invasion and represents a therapeutic vulnerability.
article.authors: Carla Pallarés-Moratalla; Mélanie Guyot; Krish Skandha Gopalan; Bernhard Robl; Jakub Idkowiak; Jonas Dehairs; Nina Ravoet; Tim F E Hendriks; Kinga Anna Nowak; Nikolina Dubroja Lakić; Linqian Weng; Vasileios Konstantakos; Xander Spotbeen; Lutgarde Serneels; Sarah-Maria Fendt; Stein Aerts; Frederik De Smet; Eva Cuypers; Johannes V Swinnen; Gabriele Bergers
article.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by diffuse infiltration into the surrounding brain, limiting complete surgical resection, the strongest determinant of patient survival. The mechanisms driving this invasive growth remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a lipid-mediated paracrine signaling axis through which tumor-associated microglia/macrophages promote glioma invasion. Integrating single-cell transcriptomics, spatial lipidomics, and functional perturbation across mouse models and human GBM samples, we show that invading tumor cells engage and reprogram myeloid cells via colony-stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF1R)-PI3K signaling. This induces lipid metabolic reprogramming and secretion of bioactive lipids, including lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and lysophosphatidic acids (LPAs), which promote GBM invasion through distinct downstream pathways. Disruption of this myeloid-GBM axis reduces lipid secretion and suppresses invasion. Targeting downstream LPA-LPA receptor (LPAR) or YAP/TAZ signaling further constrains invasion in a context-dependent manner. Together, these findings define a lipid-driven circuit linking the tumor microenvironment to glioma invasion and identify strategies to reduce infiltration and improve surgical resection.

article.title: Molecular mechanisms and therapeutic potential of Rasayana in cellular protection and healthy aging.
article.authors: Rutuja Gulhane; Neha Nistane; Mohammad Qutub; Amol Tatode; Milind Umekar; Brijesh Taksande; Jayshree Taksande
article.venue: Journal of Ayurveda and integrative medicine
article.abstract: Aging is a complex biological process characterized by oxidative stress, cellular senescence, and metabolic dysregulation. Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine, emphasizes longevity and rejuvenation through Rasayana therapy, a specialized branch that enhances vitality, delays aging, and prevents age-related diseases. This review explores the mechanistic basis of Ayurvedic antioxidants, including Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), Amalaki (Emblica officinalis), Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia), Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus), Haritaki (Terminalia chebula), Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), and Curcumin (Curcuma longa), in promoting longevity. These herbs modulate key aging pathways, including oxidative stress reduction, mitochondrial protection, immune modulation, neuroprotection, telomere maintenance, and endocrine balance. Scientific evidence highlights their potential in mitigating chronic inflammation, enhancing cognitive function, and improving metabolic homeostasis, thereby increasing lifespan and healthspan. Systematic electronic database search via PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar with the use of the keywords "Ayurveda," "Rasayana," "antioxidants," "longevity," and "anti-aging herbs" was conducted. English-language peer-reviewed papers were selected on the basis of relevance, mechanistic content, and availability of experimental or clinical evidence. The evidence was collated to identify patterns of therapy and mechanisms in common. Despite promising outcomes, the clinical translation of Ayurvedic antioxidants faces challenges such as limited standardized trials, bioavailability concerns, and regulatory hurdles. Future directions include integrating Ayurvedic principles with modern medicine through personalized therapeutics, nutraceutical innovations, and synergistic formulations. Standardized clinical trials and molecular validation are essential for their acceptance in global healthcare. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of Ayurvedic antioxidants as potent natural interventions for healthy aging.

article.title: Bisphenol A induces ACSL4-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury: Implications for Hunner-type interstitial cystitis.
article.authors: Wenbo Wu; Yang Xu; Zhongwen Lu; Yang Zhang; Liyu Cai; Feng Gao; Zhuohan Niu; Dayuan Zong; Hui Wang; Peng Xue
article.abstract: Hunner-type interstitial cystitis (HIC) is an inflammatory subtype of interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome marked by persistent urothelial injury and bladder dysfunction. Bisphenol A (BPA) can disturb redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but its relevance to HIC-associated urothelial vulnerability remains unclear. This study examined whether acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) contributes to BPA-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury. Among non-pregnant adult women, higher creatinine-corrected urinary BPA was associated with a phenotype predominantly characterized by urgency urinary incontinence (UUI), and the primary Mendelian randomization analysis suggested higher interstitial cystitis (IC) risk with genetically proxied BPA exposure. Integrated transcriptomic, BPA-target, and machine-learning analyses prioritized ACSL4 as a consistent HIC-associated candidate. HIC tissues showed higher ferro-aging-like transcriptional scores and ACSL4 expression; single-cell analyses further identified disease-associated urothelial cell-state remodeling, with higher ACSL4 expression and SenePy scores in HIC urothelial cells. Structure-based modeling suggested a plausible BPA-ACSL4 interaction, while cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) indicated BPA-associated thermal stabilization of ACSL4. In primary human urothelial cells, BPA increased ACSL4 mRNA and protein expression, lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, p21 expression, senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) positivity, inflammatory signaling, and barrier impairment, together with reduced Lamin B1 and ZO-1 expression and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). ACSL4 silencing and vitamin C attenuated these changes. In mice, PRGL493 and vitamin C each attenuated multiple BPA-induced bladder abnormalities. Together, these findings support an ACSL4-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury phenotype involving iron-lipid stress, senescence-associated changes, inflammation, and barrier impairment, with relevance to selected features of HIC.

article.title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
article.authors: Yuan Li; Nazir Ahmed; Xiaofei Li; Khadijat Ul Kubra; Dua Rubab; Tao Lang
article.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental toxicant associated with neurological injury, but the role of mitophagy remains unresolved because increased pathway markers may indicate protective clearance, broad mitochondrial selection or incomplete downstream degradation. This review evaluates mitochondrial quality-control checkpoints in Cd-exposed neural systems, focusing on PINK1-Parkin, BNIP3L/NIX and autophagy-lysosome completion, and examines intervention evidence from puerarin, daidzein and ginsenoside Rg1. Three states are proposed as a conceptual synthesis: adaptive clearance, candidate disproportionate mitochondrial elimination and initiated but stalled flux. Protective PINK1- and BNIP3L-dependent activity has loss-of-function support, whereas selection-pathway engagement accompanied by mitochondrial loss is consistent with, but does not establish, disproportionate elimination because degradation and replacement have not been measured together.
